off.p: The broken flange is the leading suspect. A wax ring normally lasts for decades; yearly failure suggests movement or an incorrect fit. Even if the toilet feels firm by hand, it may move slightly when someone sits on it. Wax compresses but doesn’t spring back, so movement can open a leak path. Oatey’s flange repair guidance
For a lasting repair:

off.li: Repair or replace the flange. If only the mounting ring is broken, a suitable repair ring anchored into sound flooring may suffice. If the drain portion or pipe connection is cracked, it needs replacement. Check for soft or rotten flooring while the toilet is off.

Make the bowl stable before installing the seal. Dry-fit it without a ring and use plastic toilet shims wherever needed to eliminate rocking. The floor should support the bowl. Korky’s installation guidance

Check flange height. Ideally, the flange sits on top of the finished floor. A recessed flange may leave a standard ring insufficiently compressed; use a suitable flange extension or the seal thickness specified for that height. Oatey’s wax-ring guidance

Reset carefully. Remove the old wax, install a fresh ring, and seat the bowl without rocking or lifting it again. Tighten the mounting nuts evenly and gently—excess tightening can crack the porcelain. Oatey’s installation instructions

off.p: Given that both ordinary and reinforced rings have failed, I’d put the effort into fixing the flange and supporting the bowl properly before trying another seal type.

on.p: The broken flange is the leading suspect. A toilet can feel firmly attached yet still move slightly under someone’s weight. That movement can break the wax seal; compressed wax cannot spring back to close the resulting gap. Oatey identifies rocking from a damaged flange as a cause of seal failure. Oatey’s flange guidance
For a lasting repair:

on.li: Repair or replace the flange. A repair ring can restore damaged bolt slots if the remaining flange and drain connection are sound. Extensive damage calls for replacement. Secure it to solid flooring, and repair any soft or rotten subfloor.
Check the flange height. A conventional flange should rest on top of the finished floor. A recessed flange may need a compatible extender so the seal compresses properly. Flange repair guide
Support the bowl evenly. Before installing the seal, dry-fit the toilet and use plastic toilet shims wherever needed to eliminate rocking. The floor and shims must support the bowl.
Install a fresh seal and tighten evenly. Seat the bowl carefully, then snug the bolts. Overtightening can crack the porcelain. If you lift the toilet after compressing the wax, use another new ring.

on.p: A properly installed wax seal should last many years. Reinforcement cannot compensate for movement or incorrect flange height. Given that yours is broken in several places, I would address the flange before buying another seal. Oatey’s wax-ring guidance

off.p: Yes—78°F indoors at 105–106°F outdoors is achievable with a properly sized, functioning central AC. But whether your particular system should maintain it depends on your local climate, the house’s heat gain, and the system’s capacity. Reaching 89°F with a 78°F setting is enough of a shortfall that I would investigate it.

AC systems are sized for a location’s *design temperature*, rather than its hottest possible day. If 106°F is well above that temperature where you live, a healthy system can run continuously and still fall behind. If temperatures like this are routine locally, maintaining 78°F is a more reasonable expectation. ENERGY STAR’s design guidance

There is no universal “20°F below outdoors” limit. The often-mentioned 20°F difference refers roughly to the temperature drop between indoor air entering the AC and cooled air leaving it. That air recirculates, so the house can become much more than 20°F cooler than outside. Carrier’s explanation

Your second day being worse despite a slightly lower outdoor high could reflect heat retained in the walls, roof, and furnishings, especially after the warmer night. That is a plausible explanation, not a diagnosis; humidity, airflow, or equipment trouble could also contribute.
A few useful checks:

off.li: Check the filter, and make sure supply vents and return grilles are open and unobstructed.
Observe the outdoor unit while the thermostat calls for cooling. An indoor fan running does not establish that the compressor is working.

Measure return-air and supply-air temperatures with an air thermometer while cooling is running steadily. A drop around 20°F is a useful rough check, but humidity and airflow affect it, and a normal drop does not prove adequate overall capacity.
Look for visible ice on refrigerant tubing or the indoor coil. If present, turn cooling off and arrange service.

off.p: Dirty filters or coils, refrigerant problems, and insufficient capacity can all cause this behavior. Carrier’s troubleshooting guidance

Given the 11°F gap from your setting, I’d arrange an HVAC check, especially if the system previously handled similar weather. Ask them to verify airflow, refrigerant charge, coil condition, and duct losses before concluding that you need a larger unit.
What city or region are you in, and does the AC recover to 78°F overnight? Those details would help distinguish extreme-weather limits from a performance problem.

on.p: Yes—78°F at 105–106°F outdoors is achievable with a properly sized, functioning central AC and a reasonably insulated home. Whether your particular system should maintain it depends on the home’s heat gain and the conditions the system was sized for.

AC sizing uses a local outdoor “design temperature.” Above that temperature, a correctly sized system may run continuously and still let the indoor temperature rise. ENERGY STAR recommends using the local temperature exceeded during only 1% of annual hours for cooling-load calculations. ENERGY STAR sizing guidance

Your 89°F indoor temperature with a 78°F setting warrants investigation. Those readings alone can’t establish whether the cause is inadequate capacity, heat entering the house, or an equipment problem. The warmer overnight low could also have left the building holding more heat going into today.

There’s no universal outdoor-to-indoor temperature difference an AC can maintain. The commonly mentioned 15–20°F temperature drop refers to air passing through the indoor cooling coil; the actual drop varies with humidity, airflow, and equipment. ACCA explanation
Useful checks:

on.li: Check the filter and airflow: replace a dirty filter and keep supply and return vents clear.
Observe operation: when the house is well above the setting, check whether the outdoor unit runs continuously and whether the vents deliver cool air.
Reduce solar heat: close blinds or curtains on sunny windows and keep vegetation and debris clear of the outdoor unit. Trane heat-wave guidance

Arrange service if it continues reaching the upper 80s: ask for checks of cooling performance, airflow, refrigerant charge, and duct condition. If the equipment performs correctly, ask for a Manual J load calculation to assess its capacity for your home. DOE diagnostic guidance, ACCA sizing methods

on.p: Your city, whether the AC runs continuously, and whether it reaches 78°F overnight would help narrow down what to expect.

off.p: Draining the pipes is usually a temporary fix. A proper water hammer arrester is the lasting fix—if water hammer is indeed the cause.

Older plumbing sometimes has capped pipe sections that trap air to cushion sudden pressure changes. Draining can replenish that air, but it gradually dissolves into the water. Your brief improvement is consistent with this, though it doesn’t prove you have those chambers. Modern arresters keep their air cushion separated from the water so they don’t become waterlogged. Sioux Chief explanation
I’d proceed in this order:

off.li: Check whether it’s hammer or valve chatter. Close the faucet slowly, then quickly. Noise primarily after a quick closure points toward water hammer. A buzzing or rapid vibration as the toilet finishes filling can also come from its fill valve or supply shutoff valve. If one toilet is the main culprit, cleaning or replacing its fill valve according to the manufacturer’s instructions is a reasonable DIY step. Fluidmaster’s noise guide

Measure your water pressure. Attach a hose-thread pressure gauge to a hose bib supplied by the same regulated plumbing as the house, with all fixtures off. If it exceeds 80 psi—about 5.5 bar—address the pressure regulator first. Partially closing the main shutoff reduces flow but does not reduce the pressure when everything is off. Watts pressure guidance

For confirmed hammer, fit an arrester near the valve causing it. Screw-on models can fit between a fixture’s shutoff valve and flexible supply hose, often allowing installation without cutting pipe. Choose one with the correct connections and follow its placement instructions. Shut off the supply and relieve pressure before disconnecting anything; check carefully for leaks afterward. An arrester at the main inlet may do little for a distant fixture. Arrester placement and operation
Check accessible pipe supports. Loose pipes can amplify the noise by striking framing. Secure them with supports suitable for the pipe material, without overtightening.

off.p: Given that both faucets and the toilet trigger it, checking house pressure first, then installing an arrester close to the worst offending fixture, is a sensible next move.

on.p: Check the water pressure, then consider a water-hammer arrester near the valve causing the noise. Draining the plumbing can give temporary relief if you have old-style air chambers: it restores their air cushion, but those chambers can fill with water again. Your two-to-three-day improvement fits that explanation, though it doesn’t confirm it. Sioux Chief’s air-chamber bulletin
Here’s a useful DIY sequence:

on.li: Check whether slow faucet closure prevents it. Water hammer occurs when flowing water stops abruptly. If closing the same faucet slowly eliminates the noise, that supports the diagnosis. A brief buzzing or chattering sound as the toilet finishes filling can also come from its fill valve or supply valve. Fluidmaster’s noise guide

Measure your household water pressure. Attach a screw-on pressure gauge to a hose tap supplied by the house plumbing, then read it with all fixtures off. If you have a pressure regulator, use a connection downstream of it. A reading above 80 psi—about 5.5 bar— calls for investigating the regulator or installing one. Adjust an existing regulator according to its instructions and recheck the gauge. Watts’ pressure-reduction guide

For confirmed hammer, install a sealed water-hammer arrester close to the offending valve. Look for an ASSE 1010-certified model with connections that match your supply. Retrofit models can fit at a toilet or faucet supply connection; placement near the source matters. Shut off the supply, relieve pressure, follow the fitting instructions, and check carefully for leaks after reopening the water. A sealed piston or diaphragm keeps the cushioning air separated from the water. Sioux Chief’s arrester explanation

If the toilet chatters as its valve closes, service or replace the fill valve. Clean it according to the manufacturer’s instructions first. Also inspect accessible pipes while someone operates the fixture; secure loose supports where pipes visibly move or strike framing.

on.p: For your symptoms, I’d start with the pressure measurement and slow-closure test. Those will help you decide whether an arrester or a toilet-valve repair is the next purchase.

off.p: The useful distinction is whether the pilot goes out while you’re still holding the lighting control, or only when you release it. A brief flame alone doesn’t establish that the thermocouple is faulty.
The Honeywell V4600C is a gas valve for a standing pilot with a thermocouple—a sensor heated by the pilot that allows the safety valve to remain open. Manufacturer’s description.
Based on that arrangement, these are the likely diagnostic branches:

off.li: It stays lit while the control is held, then goes out on release: first check the boiler’s own lighting instructions, including the specified holding time. Possible faults include insufficient flame heating the thermocouple, a faulty thermocouple or connection, or a defective valve safety unit.
It goes out even while the control is held correctly: pilot gas flow, a restricted pilot injector, or a valve fault needs investigating. Replacing the thermocouple alone may not solve this.
It rarely catches at all: the engineer should also check the igniter and its position relative to the pilot.

off.p: Your gas fire working confirms gas reaches the house. Gas at the boiler inlet doesn’t prove adequate operating pressure or flow through the pilot circuit.

Because you’ve checked the inlet pressure point, stop further attempts if that involved loosening or removing its screw. Have a Gas Safe registered engineer confirm it is sealed and leak-tight. Don’t open other gas connections, adjust the valve, clean the injector yourself, or bypass the safety device.

For your own checks, find the boiler make/model and its lighting instructions, and note what happened during your previous attempts. Given its unknown service history, arrange a service and safety check before using it; ask the engineer to check the pilot, thermocouple circuit, gas pressures, ventilation and flue. HSE guidance.

If you smell gas, avoid flames and electrical switches, ventilate, turn off the gas at the meter if safe, and call 0800 111 999 in Great Britain or 0800 002 001 in Northern Ireland. Gas Safe emergency guidance.

on.p: Given the repeated flame failure and your check at the pressure test point, leave the boiler off and arrange a Gas Safe registered engineer. If you loosened or opened that test point, tell the engineer so they can check that it is sealed and gas-tight before use.
The useful diagnostic detail is whether the flame goes out while you’re holding the pilot button down, or only after you release it:

on.li: Only after releasing it: the thermocouple may have had insufficient time to heat, the pilot flame may be too weak to heat it properly, or the thermocouple or valve’s safety magnet may be faulty.
While still holding it down: the engineer should investigate pilot gas flow, including a restricted pilot jet or tubing, and the valve’s operation.

on.p: The Honeywell V4600 family uses a thermocouple heated by the pilot to hold the safety valve open. Its handbook describes holding the button down for 20 seconds after ignition and waiting at least three minutes after a failed attempt. Your boiler’s own lighting instructions take precedence. These symptoms alone cannot establish which component has failed. Honeywell handbook, pp. 19–21.pdf)
The working gas fire confirms gas reaches that appliance. Gas at the boiler inlet does not establish adequate operating pressure or gas flow through the pilot circuit.

For now, find the boiler’s make, model and lighting instructions, and check any available service records. Leave pilot cleaning, pressure adjustments and thermocouple work to the engineer; never bypass the flame safety device. Given its unknown history, ask for a service and flue safety check as well. HSE guidance

If you smell gas or suspect a leak, stop lighting attempts, avoid electrical switches and flames, open doors and windows, turn off gas at the meter if safe, and call 0800 111 999 in Great Britain or 0800 002 001 in Northern Ireland. Gas Safe emergency guidance

off.p: Start by checking whether the door itself binds when operated by hand. The catch at a repeatable height, and the fact that pulling down helps, suggest extra mechanical resistance—but a safety-sensor fault can also cause reversal.

off.li: Test it manually while the problem is present. With the door fully closed, unplug the opener and disconnect its trolley using the release specified in the manual. Don’t release an open door; it could fall. Slowly raise and lower the door using its handle, keeping fingers clear of section joints. Feel for resistance around that two-foot position, and compare wet versus dry operation.

If it catches manually, inspect what moves or rubs at that position. Look for a sticking roller, bent track, debris, damaged hinge, or rubbing against the side trim/weather seal. Look along the entire door: a roller higher up may be causing the catch. With the rain connection, I would particularly suspect swollen wooden trim or a wooden door, or a wet seal dragging against the door. These are possibilities to confirm by finding rubbing marks or watching the contact point.

Clean and lubricate selectively. Wipe debris from the tracks; don’t pack them with grease. Lubricate hinge pivots and serviceable roller bearings as your door manufacturer specifies. If the door is unusually heavy, moves unevenly, or won’t remain roughly halfway open, have its balance and hardware checked. Leave springs, cables, and bottom cable brackets to a garage-door technician. Genie’s maintenance guidance

If it moves smoothly by hand, check the photoelectric safety sensors. Clean and dry their lenses, check alignment and loose brackets, and inspect exposed wiring for damage or moisture. Watch the indicator lights from outside the door’s path during a failed closing cycle; flickering or an error code can identify a sensor problem. Use your opener’s manual to interpret the lights. Genie’s reversal troubleshooting

off.p: Avoid increasing closing force to overcome the catch, or continuing to pull on the powered door. Locate the resistance first. After repairs or adjustments, perform the obstruction-reversal and sensor tests prescribed in your opener’s manual.

on.p: The catch at a repeatable height, and the fact that pulling helps, suggest mechanical binding. Rain could change the clearance around a wooden door or jamb, or make a rubbing weather seal more troublesome. That is a working hypothesis; a safety-sensor fault can also cause reversal.
Start with these checks:

on.li: Test the door by hand when wet. With the door fully closed, unplug the opener and disengage it according to its manual. Slowly raise and lower the door using its handle, keeping fingers clear of panel joints. Feel for resistance around the troublesome height. Disengaging an open door can let it fall if its springs are faulty. Stop if it is unusually heavy or difficult to control. Chamberlain’s manual-operation guidance

Locate the rubbing point. Look for fresh scrape marks on the door edges and jambs, tight side weatherstripping, and swollen or warped wood. Watch for a roller that stops turning or catches at a track joint. Check the entire mechanism at that door position: the troublesome roller may be well above the floor.

Clean and lubricate appropriately. Remove debris from the tracks and wipe them clean. Follow the door manual for lubricating hinge pivots and serviceable roller bearings; keep grease off the track’s rolling surfaces.

Check balance and sensors. A manually operated door should move smoothly and remain approximately halfway open. If it pulls strongly upward or drops, have a technician check the balance. If manual travel is smooth, clean and dry the photo-eye lenses, check their alignment indicators during closing, and consult the opener’s diagnostic codes. Overhead Door’s maintenance guidance

on.p: Do not increase closing force to overcome the catch or keep assisting the powered door by hand. Excess force can compromise the reversal protection. Leave spring, cable, and bottom-bracket adjustments to a garage-door technician. After repairs, perform the safety tests specified in your opener’s manual. Chamberlain’s force-adjustment warning

off.p: The attic is often a practical DIY project; insulating those exterior walls is usually a substantial renovation. The key question is whether the plaster is directly against the block or whether there is a usable cavity behind it.
Have the inspector confirm the actual wall construction. A neighbor’s experience is a useful clue, but it doesn’t establish what this particular house contains.
For the walls, there are three possible approaches:

off.li: Insulate from inside. Add a properly designed insulation and air-sealing layer, then framing or furring and drywall. This reduces room dimensions and involves adjusting window trim, baseboards, outlets, and possibly radiators or cabinets. A skilled DIYer could handle much of the carpentry and finishing, but it is a room-by-room remodeling job.

Insulate from outside. Add continuous insulation and new exterior cladding. This preserves indoor space but covers the brick and requires careful detailing around windows, doors, and roof edges. It is generally a contractor-scale project.

Fill an existing cavity, if suitable. This requires confirming that the cavity can safely be insulated. Don’t assume the gap behind brick is available—it may serve drainage—or that filling hollow block cores provides the same benefit as continuous insulation.

off.p: The first two approaches are described in DOE’s masonry retrofit guidance. Moisture design matters: interior insulation makes the masonry colder and reduces its ability to dry inward. Depending on climate and rain exposure, a poorly designed installation can cause condensation or freeze–thaw damage. Get the wall assembly specified by someone experienced with masonry retrofits before choosing insulation or a vapor barrier. DOE masonry insulation guide

The attic is where I would start, assuming it is an accessible, unfinished attic. The usual sequence is to seal leaks through the ceiling, maintain ventilation paths and required clearances around heat sources, then add blown cellulose/fiberglass or unfaced batts. ENERGY STAR estimates 1–3 days for a DIY attic project, although access and preparation can make it harder. DIY effort guide, installation guidance
Assuming U.S. dollars, rough attic budgets are:

table: Approximate cost for 1,000 sq. ft. of attic
DIY blown insulation, materials and equipment

off.p: These are broad budgeting ranges; insulation depth, air sealing, access, removal, and repairs affect the price. DIY cost estimate, installed cost estimate

For the walls, I would carry a provisional five-figure renovation allowance for a whole-house project until you obtain quotes. Insulation itself is only part of the expense; finishing, trim, electrical changes, and moisture repairs can dominate. Wall costs should be calculated using exterior wall area, rather than the home’s floor area.

Before purchasing, ask for measured attic insulation levels, evidence of wall dampness, and an energy assessment to prioritize improvements. If the attic contains vermiculite, leave it undisturbed pending professional assessment because it may contain asbestos. EPA guidance
Your location, house size, and whether you intend to remodel the rooms would help narrow the wall options and budget considerably.

on.p: The attic is often a manageable DIY project. Insulating brick-and-block walls is a substantial renovation, especially if the plaster is applied directly to the block.
First, have the inspector confirm the actual wall layers. There may be interior furring strips, an existing insulation layer, or a drainage gap behind the brick. Those details determine your options.
For the walls, the usual approaches are:

on.li: Add insulation inside. Install a designed insulation system against the masonry, then cover it with an approved interior finish, typically drywall. This reduces room dimensions and requires changes around outlets, baseboards, and window and door trim. Depending on the existing plaster’s condition, some removal may be needed.
Add continuous insulation outside, with new cladding. This changes the house’s appearance and requires careful detailing at windows, doors, roof edges, and the foundation.

Fill an existing cavity only after confirming its purpose and suitability. A gap behind brick may provide drainage; filling it can create moisture problems. Hollow concrete blocks also need assessment before considering injected insulation. DOE’s insulation renovation guide explains masonry retrofit options and their limitations.

on.p: Interior insulation changes how warm the masonry stays and how it dries. Poor detailing can cause condensation, and cold climates can introduce freeze–thaw damage. Have someone experienced with masonry retrofits specify the insulation and moisture-control details. An experienced DIYer can then tackle much of the carpentry and finishing. Building Science Corporation’s masonry retrofit guidance covers these considerations.

For an accessible, vented attic, the work generally involves sealing air leaks at the ceiling, maintaining ventilation paths at the eaves, and adding insulation to the appropriate depth. Follow required clearances around chimneys, flues, and light fixtures. DOE attic guidance recommends air sealing before insulating.

For cost, assuming U.S. dollars: HomeGuide’s 2026 estimate puts professionally installed attic insulation at roughly $1–$4 per square foot, or $1,000–$4,000 for a 1,000-square-foot attic. Removal, repairs, and substantial air sealing can add to that. DIY costs depend on the additional insulation needed and equipment rental. HomeGuide attic cost estimate

A whole-house masonry wall retrofit can reach tens of thousands of dollars once framing, finishes, electrical work, and trim are included. Treat that as a planning allowance: the description alone cannot support a reliable quote. Ask contractors to price the complete finished assembly, using wall area, rather than just the insulation material.
Before purchasing, I would ask for:

on.li: Confirmation of wall construction and attic insulation type, depth, and condition.
An assessment of leaks, damp masonry, and drainage.
An energy assessment to identify which improvements offer the best return.
Separate estimates for attic work and wall retrofits.

on.p: If the attic contains vermiculite, leave it undisturbed and get professional advice; it may contain asbestos. DOE guidance
Your location, house size, and attic access would help narrow the budget considerably.

off.p: You may not need to drain the pool. The first option is to isolate the plumbing at the pool using properly sized winterizing plugs.

off.li: Turn off power to the pump, including automatic controls.

Remove the skimmer baskets and plug the pipe openings at the bottom of the skimmers, rather than trying to cover the skimmer mouths. Use threaded plugs where the fittings accept them, or correctly sized rubber expansion plugs. Pentair describes using skimmer plugs for winterizing.

Isolate the return lines too, along with any separate main-drain or cleaner lines connected to the plumbing you’re replacing. Below-water equipment needs isolation on both suction and return sides. Pentair pump manual

off.p: A separate main-drain line can make this difficult; if it cannot be isolated with a working valve, a pool service company should handle that part. Verify that water flow stops through a controlled drain opening before cutting anything.

If you do need to lower the water, a siphon could avoid needing another pump. Fill a hose completely with water, keep its intake submerged, and place the discharge at a suitable location below the pool’s water surface. It will flow until the intake admits air or the water levels equalize. A garden hose works, but slowly.

I would avoid cutting a live line and then trying to control the flow while attaching temporary plumbing. Install working isolation valves and unions during the repair so future service is straightforward.
Also, don’t assume fully emptying the pool is safe: pool construction and groundwater conditions matter, and emptying can damage the shell or liner. Pentair’s draining caution

on.p: You may be able to do the repairs with the pool full, provided every line feeding the work area can be positively isolated. I’d try that before cutting a pipe with water behind it.

on.li: Plug the actual pipe openings in the skimmers. Remove the baskets and use correctly sized threaded winterizing plugs or rubber expansion plugs in the ports at the bottom. Blocking the skimmer mouth can still leave an air leak. Some skimmers have a second port connected to a main drain or equalizer, so identify the connections first. Plug any return jets feeding the repair area too. Pentair’s winterizing guidance and skimmer information describe these fittings.

If you need to lower the water, use a siphon. A garden hose or airtight pool vacuum hose will work if its discharge end is below the pool’s water surface. Fill the hose completely by submerging it, cover one end, move that end to a suitable discharge location, then uncover it while keeping the intake submerged. Flow stops when the water reaches the discharge elevation or air enters the hose. Pool water-level guidance
If the elevation won’t permit enough draining, rent a submersible pump. That gives you controlled drainage while leaving the existing plumbing intact.

on.p: Turn off power to the pool pump before fitting plugs, and keep it off during repairs. An unisolated main-drain line can continue flooding the equipment area even with the skimmers and returns plugged; that situation calls for a pool technician.
Avoid substantially draining an inground pool until groundwater conditions have been assessed: groundwater pressure can lift the shell. Pool & Hot Tub Alliance guidance

off.p: The box is most likely a mechanical defrost timer, if it’s mounted to the fridge’s frame beside the compressor. Without a photo or the component’s label, that identification is tentative. “ABS” identifies the plastic used for the cover, not the device inside.

A mechanical timer uses a small motor and gears to periodically switch the refrigerator from cooling to defrosting. Your description—rapid ticking while cooling still works—suggests either a noisy timer mechanism or a loose cover vibrating with the compressor. Feeling vibration in the cover alone doesn’t distinguish those causes.

A compressor start relay is another possibility, especially if the box attaches directly to the compressor’s electrical terminals. However, failed-start clicking usually accompanies interrupted compressor operation and poor cooling; your steady four-clicks-per-second sound is less typical of that fault. GE’s clicking-noise guidance
To investigate:

off.li: Unplug the fridge before removing the cover. The enclosure may contain mains-voltage connections.
Check for loose mounting screws or a cover touching nearby metal or tubing. The Y-shaped screws likely require a tri-wing bit.
Read the label on the component inside and use that, along with the full refrigerator model number, to confirm its identity.
If the timer itself is making the noise, replace the complete timer with a confirmed compatible part. If the housing is rattling, correct its mounting.

off.p: Don’t bypass the timer, leave its electrical cover off, or pack cardboard inside it. A photo showing the box and how it mounts would help distinguish the timer from the compressor’s starting components.

on.p: The white box is likely an electrical cover for the compressor’s start relay and overload protector, particularly if it attaches directly to the compressor. The relay helps start the motor; the protector cuts power if it overheats or draws excessive current. “ABS” identifies the plastic material. A photo showing the box and its connections would help confirm its function.

Four clicks per second while the fridge continues cooling suggests vibration or rattling, though a chattering relay is another possibility. The usual failed-start pattern involves a hum, a click, and a pause before another attempt, often accompanied by poor cooling. GE’s troubleshooting guide describes that pattern.
Start with these checks:

on.li: Unplug the fridge before inspecting the box. Check whether its cover is loose or touching nearby tubing or metal. Feeling vibration alone doesn’t establish that the electrical component inside is the source.
Check that the fridge stands firmly and level, with clearance from the wall. These are Frigidaire’s recommended checks for rattling. Frigidaire vibration guidance
If the cover is secure and the clicking persists, have a technician check the start device and compressor. Replace a confirmed faulty relay with the correct part for the full model number.

on.p: Avoid putting cardboard inside the electrical cover, adjusting internal screws, or running it with the cover removed. If you notice a burning smell, or the compressor repeatedly tries and fails to start, unplug it and arrange service.
Changing the temperature setting stops the cooling cycle, which explains why the noise temporarily stops; it doesn’t identify which part is making it.

off.p: Tell him to lower the finished soil level to at least 6 inches below the bottom edge of your siding, including any mulch. Virginia’s Henrico County publishes that same 6-inch siding clearance in its residential inspection guidance. Henrico County guidance

There are two related measurements: the height of the foundation above ground and the clearance beneath the siding. They can differ because siding sometimes overlaps the foundation. The IRC’s foundation provision calls for the top of a concrete or masonry foundation to be at least 6 inches above finished grade for houses with siding. ICC explanation of R404.1.6
The excavation also needs to drain:

off.li: Slope the soil away from the house, ordinarily dropping at least 6 inches over the first 10 feet.
If the brick pad or property line prevents that slope, provide a drain or swale with an outlet. Simply digging a narrow trench beside the foundation could create a water-filled trough. IRC R401.3

off.p: For your snow conditions, I’d aim for 8–12 inches of siding clearance where practical as an extra margin, rather than treating 6 inches as protection against every snowfall. Keep piled snow away from that wall.

Since you already have substantial water damage, have the lower wall opened and inspected during the repair. Lowering the soil prevents further burial; damaged sheathing, framing, and flashing still need attention.

on.p: Have him lower the finished soil level to at least 6 inches below the bottom of the siding. Aim for 8–12 inches if practical; that is the preferred clearance in the Department of Energy’s guidance. Measure from the final surface, including any mulch. DOE foundation guidance

Virginia Residential Code §R317.1 uses 6 inches above soil and 2 inches above paved surfaces as thresholds for decay protection of wood siding, sheathing, and framing. Those provisions concern wood components behind your aluminum siding too. The siding manufacturer’s instructions and the wall construction determine the precise required clearance for your assembly. Virginia Residential Code §R317.1

The excavation also needs to drain. A narrow trench beside the foundation can collect water. Virginia requires soil to fall at least 6 inches over the first 10 feet away from the house, or a drain/swale where space prevents that slope. Its current minimum slope for impervious paving is 1% away from the building. Virginia drainage requirements

For your situation, I’d specify the 6-inch minimum clearance even beside the brick pad, with additional clearance where feasible given the snow. Keep shoveled snow away from the wall. Since you already have substantial water damage, have the lower wall opened and inspected: lowering the soil addresses the exposure, but damaged sheathing, framing, and flashing still need repair.

off.p: Once latex/acrylic paint has fully dried, there may be no reliable way to remove it while preserving every affected hair. Water-based paint is easier to wash away when wet; acrylic paint forms a water-resistant film as it dries. Crayola
For anyone facing this before resorting to cutting, a gentle approach is:

off.li: Wet the affected strands with comfortably warm water and shampoo gently. Avoid vigorous rubbing.
Apply plenty of conditioner. Working on a small section, support the hair above the paint and gently roll the paint between your fingers to see whether it loosens.

Try a little plain mineral oil or olive oil on stubborn spots, then gently slide away any loosened flakes and shampoo afterward. This is a lubrication attempt, not a proven way to dissolve cured acrylic paint.
Stop if the paint remains firmly attached or the hair starts breaking. Avoid forcing a comb through painted clumps.

off.p: Conditioner reduces friction and breakage, but cannot guarantee paint removal. American Academy of Dermatology
Do not use paint thinner, turpentine, paint stripper, or other industrial solvents on your head. Solvent-containing products can irritate or burn skin and eyes. Poison Control

Your update is consistent with stubborn, cured paint: trimming the affected hair was a reasonable outcome after gentle methods failed. Repeated coloring can make hair dry and brittle, which makes aggressive removal more likely to cause breakage. However, the account alone cannot establish that hair porosity or Colorado’s climate caused the paint to stick. American Academy of Dermatology

on.p: There is no guaranteed way to remove hardened latex/acrylic paint while preserving every affected hair. Gentle loosening is worth trying; stop if it requires pulling or causes breakage.
For someone facing this problem:

on.li: Wet the affected strands with comfortably warm water and gently shampoo. Soap and water are the recommended first approach for latex paint exposure. Poison Control

Apply plenty of conditioner. Follow its recommended contact time, then gently roll individual paint flecks between your fingers. Conditioner may help loosen and slide off flecks; success with hardened paint is uncertain.

Gently comb out only loosened pieces, supporting the strand above the paint to avoid pulling at the scalp. Stop when the comb catches. Gentle handling matters because friction and force can damage fragile hair. American Academy of Dermatology
If the paint stays firmly attached, have a stylist assess selective trimming, or let the affected hair grow out.

on.p: Avoid paint stripper, paint thinner, turpentine, acetone, and WD‑40 on your hair or scalp. Household paint removers can irritate skin; their effectiveness on painted surfaces does not establish suitability for hair. Poison Control

Given your update, growing it out and cutting off the affected portions was a reasonable outcome. The delay and your hair’s condition may have contributed, but your experience alone cannot establish how much either factor mattered.

off.p: The switch changes the regeneration program—the cycle that recharges the resin with brine. A mismatch can reduce softening performance, especially if you’re using KCl with the controller set to NaCl. The exact adjustments depend on your model.
1) What does the setting change?

For example, the Morton M45 manual explicitly says the setting “adjusts the regeneration cycle times” to compensate for KCl’s different dissolution rate. It doesn’t specify which stages change or by how many minutes. So without your make and model, claiming that the switch always adds a particular amount of salt or rinse time would be guessing. Morton M45 manual, page 14

The controller needs to account for differences in brine preparation and regeneration performance. KCl can require more regenerant to achieve the same useful softening capacity. Some machines accommodate this through programming; others require manual adjustments. University of Nebraska–Lincoln Extension
2) Could an incorrect setting explain hard water?

table: Inadequate regeneration or less capacity than expected, potentially allowing hardness through before the next cycle.
Generally unnecessary regeneration compensation, potentially wasting salt, water, or time; less likely to explain persistent hard water.

off.p: Those are general expectations, rather than a diagnosis for your particular controller.
Check the bag, match the setting, and run a manual regeneration according to the manual. Then test cold water from a tap supplied by the softener, after flushing the pipe:

off.li: Soft afterward, then hard before the next regeneration: points toward insufficient capacity or incorrect regeneration settings.

Hard immediately afterward: investigate bypass position, brine delivery, and valve/resin problems. A blocked injector/venturi, for example, prevents brine reaching the resin. Morton maintenance guidance

off.p: A declining salt level indicates consumption, but doesn’t establish that regeneration is effective. Your make and model would let us identify precisely what that toggle changes.

on.p: The toggle changes the regeneration program. A mismatch can cause inadequate regeneration, particularly when you use KCl with the controller set to NaCl. The exact changes depend on your model.
1. What does the setting change?
For a documented example, the Whirlpool WHES48 manual says selecting KCl increases the fill and brine-rinse times. Manufacturer’s manual, page 20
That means:

on.li: Longer fill: More water enters the salt tank to make the required volume of regenerating brine.
Longer brine draw/rinse: The valve allows more time to pull that brine through the resin and rinse it out.

on.p: KCl has different solubility characteristics, including greater sensitivity to temperature. The controller compensates by adjusting the amount of water and cycle timing. EcoWater’s patent describing this control method explains these adjustments.
Your model’s manual is needed to establish exactly which timings change and by how much.
2. Could the wrong setting explain hard water?
The direction of the mismatch matters:

table: May deliver too little regenerant, leaving the resin incompletely regenerated and reducing how much water it can soften between cycles.
Generally uses extra salt and water; this mismatch alone would be unlikely to explain persistent hard water.

on.p: Those are expected consequences of the dosing changes, rather than a diagnosis of your particular unit.

Check the salt bag, match the setting, then run a complete manual regeneration following your manual. Afterward, flush and test a cold-water tap supplied by the softener. Whirlpool recommends testing cold faucets after regeneration in its hard-water troubleshooting guide.

If the water becomes soft but turns hard before the next regeneration, insufficient regeneration or an incorrect hardness/capacity setting becomes more plausible. If it remains hard immediately afterward, check the bypass position and whether brine is actually being drawn through the resin. A falling salt level shows salt consumption; successful softening still needs to be confirmed by a hardness test.
What make and model is your softener?

off.p: A water-filled siphon over the tank rims can equalize the levels without drilling the tanks. Unlike a temporary transfer, it can stay in place and resume flowing whenever one tank’s water surface becomes higher than the other. This uses the principle demonstrated by Iowa State University’s siphon experiment.
With the owner’s agreement:

off.li: Run an airtight, drinking-water-rated hose or pipe over the rims, with one end near the bottom of each tank.
Fill it completely with water, removing all air bubbles.
Keep both ends closed while positioning them underwater, then open them. Prime it by filling or using a suitable pump, rather than sucking by mouth.

off.p: Water will flow from the higher water surface toward the lower one and stop when their elevations match, assuming both tanks are vented to the atmosphere. Equal elevation means equal depth only if the tank bottoms are at the same elevation.
There are two practical limitations:

off.li: Both ends must remain submerged. If either tank exposes an end, or air enters or accumulates in the pipe, the siphon can fail and need priming again.
During filling or use, a small level difference is necessary to drive flow. A narrow hose may not transfer water fast enough to keep the levels close.

off.p: Being on a three-storey roof does not change this principle; the relevant height is the pipe’s crest above the water surfaces.

For dependable long-term operation, your proposed bottom connection is better. For drinking water, have a plumber assess the connection and supply backflow protection, since interconnected storage systems can introduce contamination pathways. See EPA’s guidance.

on.p: A permanently primed siphon can equalize the two tanks. Run a hose up over their rims, with both ends submerged, preferably near the bottom. Assuming both tanks are vented to the atmosphere, water will flow from the higher water surface to the lower one until their surfaces reach the same elevation. It can flow either way as water is added or used.
To set it up:

on.li: Fill the hose completely with water, removing all air. This is called *priming*. FAO siphon instructions.
Seal both ends temporarily, place one end underwater in each tank, then open them while submerged.
Secure the ends so they stay below the lowest expected water level. Keep the hose’s highest point close to the tank rims.

on.p: Once the levels equalize, flow stops, but the filled hose remains ready to transfer water when a difference develops.

The limitation is loss of prime: if either end becomes exposed, or air accumulates at the top, the siphon can stop and need priming again. An unsecured end rising above the water is a common cause. University of Washington demonstration.

The levels will also differ slightly during transfer: a difference in water level drives the flow, and a narrow hose may transfer water too slowly to keep up with use. A bottom connection is the more dependable permanent arrangement.

Being on a three-storey building makes little difference; the relevant height is the hose’s crest above the tank water surface. Agree on the connection with the owner, since it will let either household draw from both tanks.

off.p: Bare drywall: yes—prime it before painting. Once the joints are finished, dry, and sanded, remove the dust and apply a drywall primer, commonly PVA. This equalizes absorption between the drywall paper and joint compound, helping prevent patchy color and sheen. Sherwin-Williams primer guidance.

Existing painted, textured walls: you don’t always need primer before mudding. If the paint is firmly attached, clean, and dull, joint compound can generally bond to the prepared surface. Remove loose paint or texture, clean off grease and dirt, let dry, and lightly sand glossy paint to dull the sheen. USG surface-preparation guidance.

If the surface has adhesion problems, stains, or exposed torn drywall paper, use an appropriate bonding primer, stain blocker, or problem-surface sealer before mudding; follow its instructions for compatibility with joint compound. Ordinary PVA drywall primer serves a different purpose.
After skim-coating, prime again before painting. Let the compound dry completely, sand, remove dust, then prime the entire skim-coated surface for an even finish. USG finishing instructions.

on.p: Bare drywall: yes, prime before painting. Once the joints and patches are finished, completely dry, and sanded, remove the dust and apply a drywall primer. It equalizes absorption between the drywall paper and joint compound, helping prevent patchy color and sheen. Gypsum Association guidance

Existing painted, textured walls: priming before mudding depends on the surface. Sound, clean paint can usually accept joint compound after scuffing and thorough dust removal; USG recommends that preparation for previously painted wallboard. Remove loose paint or texture and clean off grease first. USG customer-service guidance

For glossy paint that you cannot thoroughly dull—particularly in the texture’s recesses—use a bonding primer approved for the surface and for application beneath joint compound. Stains need an appropriate stain-blocking primer. Follow your compound’s preparation instructions.
After you skim coat, prime again before painting: let the mud dry completely, sand it, remove the dust, then prime the entire skimmed surface. USG finishing guidance

off.p: Assuming a typical UK domestic gutter: aim for about 30mm or less where practical, and treat 50mm as a maximum only if your gutter manufacturer permits it. Neither figure guarantees that the gutter will catch the water: its width, position beneath the tiles and the roof pitch also matter.

FloPlast’s installation guide specifically says to fit the outlet no more than 50mm below the roof tiles. That is a maximum at the low point, rather than a target gap along the whole run. Without seeing your 30mm guide, I cannot tell whether it is a stricter recommendation or relates to a different system. FloPlast installation guide

The main reason for limiting the gap is water overshooting the front of the gutter. Water leaving the tiles in heavy rain has forward momentum; lowering the gutter gives it more distance to travel outward before reaching gutter height. Marley explicitly warns against lowering the gutter so far that this happens. Marley installation guidance
For your installation:

off.li: Use a modest fall. FloPlast specifies a maximum gradient of 1:350, approximately 3mm per metre. Over an 8m run that means about 23mm of drop. A 20mm gap at the high end would therefore become approximately 43mm at the outlet if the tiles were level. FloPlast FAQs
Set a string line and check the gap along the entire roof edge, including uneven tiles. Keep a consistent fall toward the outlet; following each tile’s irregularity could introduce dips.
If the required fall makes the gutter too low, consider a central outlet or another downpipe to shorten the falling runs.
Check the horizontal overlap too. The tile drip edge must sit comfortably over the gutter opening. A small vertical gap cannot compensate for poor horizontal positioning.

off.p: I would also fit the felt support trays while replacing the gutters if practical. Their purpose is to support the underlay and discharge water from beneath the tiles into the gutter; they do not cure overshooting runoff from the tile surface. Make sure the eventual tray edge will drain inside the gutter. BMI underlay support tray

on.p: Use your gutter manufacturer’s maximum, and aim for a smaller gap where practical. For a typical UK PVC gutter, FloPlast specifies fitting the outlet no more than 50 mm below the roof tiles. A 30 mm limit gives more allowance against water missing the gutter, but neither figure guarantees that every roof arrangement will work. FloPlast installation guide

The main reason is water overshooting the front edge. Water leaving a tile has outward momentum; a lower gutter gives it more time to travel outward before reaching the gutter opening. Roof pitch, tile overhang and gutter width therefore affect the acceptable gap. The tile ends should discharge approximately into the centre of the gutter. Marley roofing guidance
For your replacement, I would:

on.li: Aim for about 30 mm or less where practical, subject to the chosen system’s instructions and clearance from the tiles.
Check the gap along the whole run, particularly at the outlet and beneath tiles that sit higher. Uneven tiles can make the largest gap occur somewhere unexpected.
Use the specified fall. FloPlast recommends 1:350, approximately 2.9 mm per metre. An 8 m run therefore needs about 23 mm of total fall. Set brackets with a taut string line or laser.

If that fall makes the low end too far below the tiles, consider a central outlet or additional downpipe to shorten the drainage runs. FloPlast also permits level installation, provided the system has sufficient capacity. FloPlast technical guidance, §15.10

on.p: Plan the felt support tray now, ideally fitting it with the gutters. Its purpose is to support the underlay and discharge water from beneath the tiles into the gutter. It must overlap correctly beneath the underlay and reach the gutter; it does not solve water overshooting from the tile tops. FloPlast eaves protection guidance
A hose test before finalising the installation can reveal obvious misses and pooling, though heavy, wind-driven rain remains a tougher test.

off.p: Treat the switch as live until it has been properly tested, and don’t wallpaper over it. A switch can have live wires behind it even when it is “off” or no longer operates a light.
To establish whether it is safe, an electrician will:

off.li: Identify the circuit supplying the switch and isolate it at the breaker/fuse box.
Secure it against someone switching it back on.
Check all conductors at the switch with a suitable two-pole voltage tester, checking that the tester works before and after testing.

off.p: A non-contact voltage pen or neon screwdriver cannot reliably prove that wiring is dead. Because testing requires access to potentially live terminals, leave the cover fitted if you’re unfamiliar with electrical work. Electrical Safety First’s safe-isolation guidance.
For your wallpapering, ask an electrician to trace and decommission the unwanted switch. There are two practical outcomes:

off.li: Wiring or connections remain: fit a proper, accessible blank cover plate and wallpaper around it.
You want a completely smooth wall: have the redundant wiring permanently disconnected and the box removed or made suitable for concealment before patching and wallpapering.

off.p: Simply leaving the breaker off does not permanently decommission the wiring. Requirements vary by location; electrical boxes containing connections generally need to remain accessible. NFPA guidance on box accessibility.

on.p: Treat the switch as live until it has been properly tested. Don’t wallpaper over it or bury its wiring just because it appears unused. A switch can have live wires even when it is off or operates no visible light.
To establish whether it is safe:

on.li: Identify and switch off the supplying circuit breaker at the fuse box/consumer unit. Keep anyone from switching it back on. Circuit labels and a light going out are only clues; they don’t prove every wire at the switch is dead.

Have the wiring tested for absence of voltage. An electrician uses a suitable two-pole voltage tester, checks that the tester works before and after testing, and checks all relevant conductors. A non-contact “voltage pen” or neon screwdriver cannot reliably prove that wiring is dead. These precautions are covered by Electrical Safety First’s safe-isolation guidance.

on.p: Since you don’t know what this switch supplies, leave the faceplate fitted and have an electrician trace it before removal. Switching off a breaker temporarily does not permanently decommission the wiring.
For the wallpapering, there are two practical options:

on.li: Keep an accessible cover: the electrician removes the switch, safely terminates any remaining wiring in the box, and fits a blanking plate. Wallpaper around the plate, leaving it removable.
Make the wall smooth: the electrician permanently disconnects or removes the redundant wiring and confirms that the box can safely be removed and the opening filled.

on.p: Ordinary boxes containing electrical connections need to remain accessible; local rules determine the permitted arrangements. NFPA’s guidance on box access explains this requirement for US installations.
What country are you in? That will help establish the rules for permanently removing it.

off.p: Leave the breaker off and don’t keep resetting it. The tripping indicates a fault, likely a short circuit. Before anyone touches the wiring, power must be shut off and verified absent with a suitable tester. ESFI safety guidance

Two black and two white ceiling wires aren’t enough information to determine the connections safely. In older switch-loop wiring, a white wire can carry hot power instead of being neutral. Connecting all wires by color can therefore create a short.

One possible arrangement is a power-supply cable plus a cable carrying power to and from the switches. In that arrangement, one connection at the ceiling feeds the switches, while a separate wire returns switched power to the lamp. Your description does not establish which wire serves each purpose.
Once the wires are positively identified, the new fixture’s connections are:

table: Verified switched hot from the switches
Verified equipment ground, with required fixture/box bonding

off.p: The existing 3-way switches can continue controlling a fixture with just those three leads. Any splice supplying the switches must also be preserved.

The old fixture’s “little metal tab” does not establish how the ceiling wires should be grouped. Because the original connections have been disturbed and the breaker now trips, have a qualified electrician trace the ceiling and switch wiring and check for damage before reconnecting it. Don’t try alternate combinations to see which works.

on.p: Leave the breaker off and stop resetting it. The tripping indicates a fault; your connections may have created a short circuit. Before touching any wires, verify that power is off with a suitable tester. ESFI safety guidance

Wire colors alone cannot establish the correct connections here. In an older switch loop, a white wire can carry hot power. Joining all the whites and all the blacks can therefore connect hot directly to neutral when the switches operate.
The new fixture needs these connections, once the ceiling wires have been positively identified:

table: Switched hot returning from the switches

on.p: The existing two switches can still control a fixture with one black and one white lead. The switching happens upstream of the fixture. Leviton wiring diagrams

One possible arrangement uses one ceiling cable for the supply and another to feed the switches and return switched power. That arrangement requires a separate splice between the supply hot and the switch feed. Your description does not identify which wires perform those functions, and the “little metal tab” needs identification too.

Because the original connections have been disturbed and the breaker has repeatedly tripped, have an electrician trace the cables, identify the conductors, and check for damage before reconnecting the fixture. A green screw provides grounding only when it connects to a verified grounding path.

off.p: Choose a dimmer that is compatible with your exact LED bulb model. “Dimmable” doesn’t mean a bulb works with every dimmer.
Check these three things:

off.li: Bulb compatibility: Look up the bulb manufacturer’s recommended dimmers or compatibility list, using the model number on the bulb or packaging.

Dimming type: Many LED GU10 bulbs suit a trailing-edge LED dimmer, but some require leading-edge control. Follow the bulb manufacturer’s specification; either type can be designed for LEDs. Varilight’s LED dimmer guide

LED load limits: Add up the bulbs’ actual wattages—not their “halogen equivalent” figures. Six 5 W bulbs make a 30 W load. Check the dimmer’s minimum and maximum LED load and any limit on the number of bulbs. Its halogen rating alone doesn’t establish LED compatibility. Lutron’s load guidance

off.p: Your flickering could be caused by an incompatible dimmer, but it could also mean the LED load is too small for the existing dimmer. If it flickers only near minimum brightness, a compatible dimmer’s minimum-brightness adjustment may resolve it. Lutron’s troubleshooting guidance
If you share the bulb make/model, the number of bulbs, and your country, I can help identify a suitable dimmer.

on.p: Choose an LED-rated dimmer that is listed as compatible with your exact bulb model. “Dimmable” means the bulb supports dimming, but compatibility still depends on the dimmer. Manufacturers publish tested bulb–dimmer combinations. Lutron compatibility guidance
Check these details before buying:

on.li: Dimming type: Look in the bulb’s datasheet for *leading-edge* or *trailing-edge* dimming. Trailing-edge LED dimmers are a common choice, but some LEDs require leading-edge control; follow the bulb manufacturer’s recommendation. Varilight’s dimmer guide

LED load range: Add up the bulbs’ actual wattages. For example, six 5 W bulbs make a 30 W load. Check that against the dimmer’s LED-specific minimum and maximum ratings, plus any maximum bulb count. Use the actual wattage printed on the bulbs, not their “50 W equivalent” figure. Lutron load guidance
Minimum-brightness adjustment: A dimmer with an adjustable minimum level can help if the bulbs flicker only near the bottom of the dimming range. Lutron troubleshooting guidance

on.p: Your flickering is consistent with an incompatible dimmer or a load below its minimum. It can also occur when the dimmer takes the bulbs below their supported brightness range, so flickering alone doesn’t establish the cause.

Have an electrician replace the wall dimmer if you’re unsure about mains wiring. If you share the bulb brand/model, how many bulbs are on the switch, and your country, I can help check suitable dimmers.

off.p: People do use foam in attics, but for a conventional vented attic, its extra cost often buys little benefit. The key distinction is whether you’re insulating the attic floor or the roof.

For attic-floor insulation, fiberglass or cellulose is usually economical because there’s room for a thick layer. Blown insulation also fits around joists, wiring and other obstructions without cutting and sealing lots of rigid boards. Foam’s greater insulation value per inch is more useful where space is limited. DOE insulation guide
Foam has a few additional caveats:

off.li: Rigid boards require careful fitting and sealing. Gaps between boards and around framing can undermine their performance.
Spray foam depends heavily on installation quality and makes later access to covered components harder.
Foam plastics have fire-protection requirements. Depending on the product and attic’s use, an approved barrier or protective coating may be required. Residential Spray Foam Guide

off.p: Spray foam under the roof deck is a different project. It’s commonly used to create an unvented attic within the home’s thermal enclosure, which can benefit HVAC equipment and ducts located there. That requires a coordinated design for ventilation, humidity and vapor control; an unsuitable assembly can accumulate moisture at the roof sheathing. Building Science guidance

For your upgrade, assuming an ordinary vented attic, I’d generally air-seal the ceiling first, then add blown cellulose or fiberglass, keeping the soffit ventilation paths clear. Small amounts of foam are useful for sealing suitable gaps even when the bulk insulation is fibrous. DOE air-sealing guidance
Check the target for your climate before settling on R-30: current U.S. recommendations reach R-49 or R-60 in many regions. ENERGY STAR recommended R-values

on.p: People do use both rigid foam and spray foam in attics. For a typical vented attic, though, fiberglass or cellulose usually offers a simpler, cheaper way to add insulation.
The key distinction is where you insulate:

on.li: At the attic floor: The attic stays outside the heated/cooled space, and its vents remain open. Batts or blown insulation work well here. Spray foam also works; one established approach uses a thin layer of closed-cell foam for air sealing, topped with loose-fill insulation. PNNL attic-floor guidance

Along the roof’s underside: Spray foam can bring the attic inside the insulated enclosure. This typically involves converting it to an unvented attic, insulating the gable walls, and providing humidity control. That can be useful when HVAC equipment and ducts are in the attic, but it requires a coordinated design. PNNL roof insulation guidance

on.p: For your upgrade, foam has several tradeoffs:

Rigid foam costs more and takes fitting work. Cutting boards around joists, braces, and wiring takes time, and seams need sealing if the boards are to control air leakage. Boards are particularly useful for attic hatches and other localized applications. In a spacious attic, adding depth with loose-fill insulation is straightforward. DOE Energy Saver guide

Spray foam needs careful preparation and installation. Existing insulation and dust generally need removing from the surfaces being sprayed. Correct mixing, application thickness, and surface conditions matter. Foam also makes later access to anything it covers more difficult; electrical junction boxes must remain accessible. PNNL attic-floor guidance

Foam has fire and moisture requirements. Exposed foam may need an approved ignition or thermal barrier, depending on the product, attic use, and local code. Roof-deck installations also need climate-appropriate vapor control to prevent moisture accumulating in the roof sheathing. Open-cell and closed-cell foam behave differently in this respect. PNNL roof insulation guidance

Assuming yours is an ordinary vented attic, I’d start by air-sealing the ceiling penetrations, maintaining clear ventilation paths at the eaves, and adding blown cellulose or fiberglass. Blown insulation fits around irregular framing and can cover the joists continuously. Batts are also suitable if fitted carefully. DOE attic air-sealing guidance, blown insulation guidance
Check the recommended total R-value for your climate before settling on R-30; your location may justify more. ENERGY STAR recommendations

off.p: You can often fix this without touching the glass tile, but the remedy depends on what is protruding. The switch toggle and the thickness of the cover plate normally project; the back edge of the plate should sit against the tile.

off.li: Turn off the disposal circuit at the breaker and verify that power is off before removing the cover or adjusting the switch.

If the switch sits too far forward, check for excessive spacers or an incorrectly fitted box extender behind its metal mounting strap. Correcting those may let the cover sit against the backsplash. Don’t force it inward or overtighten screws against glass.
If the electrical box itself projects beyond the tile, an electrician needs to reposition it. Access through the wall behind it, if available, may avoid disturbing the backsplash.
If tile or hardened adhesive obstructs the switch, have the tile installer correct the opening. Chiseling installed glass mosaic can crack adjacent pieces.

off.p: A box extender generally brings a recessed box forward, so adding one won’t solve a switch that already sticks out. Also, don’t push the assembly arbitrarily deep: U.S. electrical rules generally limit box setback behind noncombustible tile to ¼ inch. NFPA guidance, §314.20

Since the backsplash is newly installed, ask the installer to return and coordinate with an electrician if the box needs moving. A photo showing the gap around the cover—and, with power verified off, the mounting beneath it—would help identify the specific fix.

on.p: You may be able to fix this by adjusting the switch mounting, with the glass tile left intact. The cover plate should sit against the tile; the toggle or rocker normally projects beyond it.
Turn off the disposal circuit at the breaker and verify that power is off before removing the cover plate. Leviton’s safety instructions require both steps.
With the cover removed, the cause determines the repair:

on.li: The switch sits too far forward: Check for loose mounting screws or excessive spacers behind its metal mounting strap. Adjust the mounting so the switch is firmly supported at the finished wall surface.
The electrical box or an extension ring projects beyond the tile: An electrician should reposition the box or fit the correct extension. Tightening the cover screws will not correct the box depth.
Tile or grout interferes with the mounting hardware: Have the tile installer correct the opening. Avoid prying against or grinding the glass yourself.

on.p: Do not force the plate flat by overtightening its screws—that can crack the plate or put pressure on the glass. A box extender is intended for a box recessed behind the finished wall; it brings the device forward. Arlington’s description explains that function.
A photo from the side showing the gap, plus one with the cover removed after verifying power is off, would help identify which adjustment you need.

off.p: Use recessed fixtures designed for sloped ceilings, or adjustable “gimbal”/“eyeball” lights, so you can aim the beam down toward the sink. A fixed light mounted flush with the slope generally aims perpendicular to the ceiling, which can send much of its light away from the work area.
Check the lights you already bought before installing them:

off.li: Adjustment range: The fixture must tilt far enough to compensate for your ceiling’s slope. Some dedicated slope fixtures accommodate approximately 10°–45°. HALO’s sloped-ceiling housing is one example.

Compatibility: If your lights use separate housings and trims, check whether the manufacturer offers an approved adjustable or slope-specific trim for that housing. A trim swap may be enough; some installations require a different housing.

off.p: Placement matters just as much as aiming. Locate the sink light over the basin or work surface, in front of where you stand. A light behind you will cast your own shadow onto the sink even if it points straight down.

To reduce remaining shadows, overlap light from nearby fixtures rather than relying on one narrow spotlight. Add under-cabinet lighting for counters beneath upper cabinets; ceiling lights often cannot reach those surfaces well.

Before cutting the ceiling openings, have your electrician temporarily position and aim a fixture. Stand at the sink and check the illumination and glare. With a high ceiling, the fixture’s output and beam spread also matter, so there’s no reliable universal spacing rule.

on.p: Use recessed fixtures designed for sloped ceilings, and position the sink light directly above the basin. A fixed downlight mounted flush with a slope generally sends its beam perpendicular to the ceiling, which can put the brightest light away from your work area.
Since you already have the lights, check the model’s installation instructions before cutting holes:

on.li: Check whether they accept adjustable “gimbal” or “eyeball” trims, or a dedicated sloped-ceiling trim. The housing, light module, and trim must be compatible. Some fixtures require a complete sloped-ceiling housing.

Match the adjustment range to your ceiling’s pitch. To point vertically downward from a ceiling inclined 30° from horizontal, the light needs approximately 30° of tilt. Purpose-built fixtures accommodate specified slopes; for example, HALO’s slope system covers approximately 10°–45°. HALO specifications

on.p: The layout also matters:

on.li: Over the sink: locate the fixture vertically above the basin and aim it down into the sink. A light behind you can cast your head and shoulders’ shadow onto the work.

Along counters: place ceiling lights over the working surface or near its front edge. Upper cabinets can still block ceiling light, so add under-cabinet lighting where applicable. Lutron’s task-lighting guidance
Across the kitchen: use overlapping light coverage. Have the supplier check beam spread and light output at the actual ceiling-to-counter distance; a high vault needs a layout suited to that height.

on.p: Before the ceiling is finished, have your electrician temporarily power a sample fixture safely at the proposed position. Stand at the sink and check the illumination while working with your hands. That will reveal shadows and glare while the layout is still easy to change.
If you share the fixture model, ceiling pitch, and height above the sink, I can help determine whether the lights you bought are suitable.

off.p: A failed thermocouple is a likely cause, but this symptom alone doesn’t prove it needs replacing.

Holding the knob down manually opens the pilot gas valve. Once you release it, the heated thermocouple must generate enough electrical current to keep the safety valve open. If that signal is insufficient—or the valve cannot hold—the gas shuts off immediately. Two minutes would ordinarily be enough warm-up time; follow your furnace’s lighting instructions. Resideo gas-control manual
The main possibilities are:

off.li: A worn or failed thermocouple.
A weak or misdirected pilot flame that isn’t adequately heating the thermocouple tip, potentially from a dirty pilot opening.
A loose thermocouple connection at the gas valve.
A faulty safety mechanism inside the gas valve. Carrier pilot-light guidance, Resideo troubleshooting

off.p: You can visually check whether the pilot burns steadily blue and surrounds the thermocouple tip. Have an HVAC technician check the flame, connection, and thermocouple output before replacing parts. Replacement is warranted if its output is inadequate despite proper flame heating. Meanwhile, leave the furnace control off; never wedge the knob down or bypass the safety device.
If you smell gas, stop trying to light it, leave the building without operating electrical switches, and call your gas supplier’s emergency number from outside. Gas-emergency guidance

on.p: A failed thermocouple is a likely cause, but the symptom alone doesn’t confirm it. Holding the knob down manually opens the pilot gas valve. Once you release it, the heated thermocouple must produce enough electrical voltage to keep the safety valve open.
Two minutes usually exceeds the required warm-up time; for example, Resideo’s lighting instructions specify about one minute. Possible causes include:

on.li: A weak or misdirected pilot flame that doesn’t heat the thermocouple tip adequately.
A loose thermocouple connection or a failed thermocouple.
A faulty safety mechanism in the gas valve.

on.p: Check your furnace’s lighting instructions and, through the normal viewing opening, whether the pilot flame reaches the thermocouple tip. An HVAC technician can check the flame, connection, and thermocouple voltage to determine which part needs replacing. Resideo’s troubleshooting guidance calls for voltage testing when the pilot keeps going out upon release.

For now, turn the control to OFF. Never wedge the knob down or bypass the safety device. If you smell gas, leave immediately, avoid electrical switches and flames, and call your gas utility’s emergency line from outside. Gas-leak safety guidance

off.p: The most likely cause is a missing jumper between RH and RC. On many Hunter thermostats, RH supplies the heating circuit, while RC supplies the independent fan circuit. With power connected only to RH, the heat can work while “Fan ON” does nothing.

For a three-wire, single-transformer system like yours, Hunter’s instructions specify keeping the RH–RC jumper installed, with the existing wires connected to RH, G, and W/B. See the Hunter wiring instructions, page 3.
Turn off power to the furnace before checking or changing the wiring, and confirm the jumper arrangement in your exact model’s manual. Then restore power and try “Fan ON.”

The blower running during heating doesn’t prove the G connection works: the furnace can start the blower itself. If the jumper is already present, the next things to check are a loose G connection, whether that wire connects to G at the furnace, and the thermostat’s fan switch.

on.p: First check the jumper between RH and RC. On Hunter models with those terminals, a system with one R/RH supply wire needs that jumper—even with heating only. A missing jumper can leave the heating circuit working while the manual fan circuit has no power. Hunter’s manual specifically shows the jumper for a three-wire, heat-only system. Hunter wiring instructions

The blower running during heating is consistent with this: a gas or oil furnace normally starts its own blower after warming up. Selecting Fan ON uses the separate G fan-control circuit. Hunter fan-operation instructions
To check:

on.li: Turn off power to the furnace before touching the wiring.
Check your thermostat’s model-specific instructions and confirm the required RH–RC jumper is installed securely.
Check that the G wire is secure at the thermostat and connects to G at the furnace. Identify wires by their terminal connections; colors alone are unreliable. Hunter installation manual
Restore power and try Fan ON.

on.p: If the jumper and G connections are correct, an HVAC technician can test the thermostat’s fan output and the furnace’s fan-control circuit.
What is the Hunter model number, and is there currently a jumper connecting RH to RC?

off.p: For a continuous floor at the same height, the installer needs to correct the subfloor height difference before laying the laminate. The laminate itself won’t bridge a substantial step safely.
There are three usual options:

off.li: Raise the lower areas: Add securely fastened plywood of the appropriate thickness in the living room and hallway to match the dining area. With the layers you describe, this is a likely approach.
Lower the dining area: Remove extra plywood if it is unnecessary underlayment. The installer must first establish that those layers aren’t needed structurally or supporting cabinets.

Keep the different heights: Install the laminate separately on each side and use a matching reducer transition strip at the change. You can use the same flooring throughout, but there will be a visible transition. Shaw’s transition guidance

off.p: After matching heights, the installer may still need to address small dips or uneven seams. Laminate needs a firm, flat base within the particular manufacturer’s tolerances; extra layers of soft foam padding are not a substitute for this preparation. Pergo installation instructions

Have the installer inspect the exposed floors and include the preparation in the quote before installation starts. Ask specifically whether the finished rooms will be at one height, and have them check door clearance, adjoining floors, and kitchen appliance clearance—especially whether the dishwasher can still be removed.

on.p: To get the same finished height throughout, the installer will need to correct the height difference before laying the laminate. Using the same laminate in every room will leave the existing difference in place.
There are three main options:

on.li: Raise the lower areas: Add appropriately sized plywood to the living room and hallway, securely fastened to the existing subfloor. For a difference caused by extra plywood layers, this is often a practical solution.
Lower the dining area: Remove the extra plywood layers if inspection confirms they are removable underlayment and aren’t needed for structural support.

Keep the different heights: Install separate sections of laminate and join them with a reducer transition strip rated for the measured difference. Matching profiles are available for this purpose. Quick-Step transition profiles

on.p: After addressing the overall height difference, the installer may need to smooth smaller irregularities with a compound approved for plywood. Laminate needs a firm, flat supporting surface; the exact flatness requirement comes from your flooring’s installation instructions. Quick-Step installation guidance
Don’t use stacked foam underlay to make up the missing plywood height. Excess cushioning can let the boards flex and strain their locking joints.

Have the installer inspect and measure the exposed floors before installation, explain the proposed solution, and include preparation costs in the quote.
