If they raise the lower areas, they should also check door clearances and kitchen appliance clearance—particularly whether the dishwasher can still be removed.

off.p: Houseplants can absorb some pollutants, but ordinary numbers of them won’t meaningfully clean your apartment’s air. Get them because you enjoy them; investigate the headaches separately.

The quantitative evidence answers your “small forest” question. A review of 12 studies found that plants removed volatile organic compounds in small sealed chambers, but very slowly. Matching the pollutant removal provided by typical building ventilation would require approximately 10–1,000 plants per square metre. Your 670-square-foot apartment is about 62 m²: that translates to roughly 620–62,000 plants. This is a comparison with ventilation, not a prescription or a guarantee of healthy air. Cummings and Waring, 2020

The headaches deserve attention before experimenting with air cleaners. Carbon monoxide is odorless and can cause headaches. Make sure you have working CO alarms, particularly if the building has fuel-burning heating, water heaters, or cooking appliances. If an alarm sounds—or you suspect CO because of headaches with dizziness, nausea, weakness, or other occupants becoming ill—get outside immediately and seek emergency help. A recurring headache associated with the apartment also warrants medical advice. CDC guidance
For the apartment, I’d proceed in this order:

off.li: Have the landlord check ventilation and possible sources. The fact that closing the windows triggers the problem makes inadequate fresh-air exchange worth investigating, though it doesn’t identify the cause. Ask about functioning exhaust fans, outdoor-air provision, combustion appliances, and dampness. Many residential heating and cooling systems simply recirculate indoor air. Ventilate with clean outdoor air when conditions allow. EPA guidance

Use a HEPA purifier if dust or other particles are a concern. It can remove airborne particles; it won’t supply fresh air or resolve CO₂ buildup. For a single open 670-square-foot space with an eight-foot ceiling, extrapolating EPA’s sizing table gives a particle CADR of approximately 435 cubic feet per minute. Separate bedrooms may need separate units. Check CADR and noise at the speed you’ll actually use, rather than relying on advertised coverage alone. EPA air-cleaner guide

Treat gases as a different problem. HEPA doesn’t remove formaldehyde or other gases. Gas filtration requires suitable adsorbent media; EPA notes that activated carbon works best when there is a substantial amount of it. A thin carbon sheet offers limited capacity. Avoid devices that intentionally generate ozone. EPA air-cleaner guide

off.p: A genuine NDIR CO₂ monitor can help you see whether ventilation is poor while the apartment is occupied. It measures a ventilation indicator, not overall air safety, and it cannot detect carbon monoxide or formaldehyde. HSE guidance on CO₂ monitoring
The flooring and ceiling are clues, but neither establishes the cause:

off.li: Laminate flooring: Some products emit formaldehyde, with emissions depending on the product, temperature, humidity, and ventilation. Five weeks without improvement doesn’t rule out continuing emissions. If symptoms persist, seek a building assessment and targeted testing rather than assuming formaldehyde is responsible. EPA laminate-flooring guidance

Popcorn ceiling: Older textured ceilings may contain asbestos. Leave an intact ceiling undisturbed; if it is crumbling or shedding, report it and arrange professional assessment before scraping or sampling it. EPA asbestos guidance

off.p: A purifier is much more realistic than plants for reducing dust, but checking CO and getting the ventilation assessed are the priorities given your headaches.

on.p: Houseplants can absorb some pollutants, but ordinary numbers of potted plants won’t meaningfully clean your apartment’s air. A HEPA air cleaner can help with dust; the headaches and rapid stuffiness also warrant checking the apartment’s ventilation and possible pollution sources.

A useful quantitative answer comes from Cummings and Waring’s review, published online in 2019. They analyzed 196 results from 12 studies and estimated that 10–1,000 plants per square metre would be needed to match the VOC removal provided by typical building ventilation. Your 670-square-foot apartment is about 62 square metres: that translates to roughly 620–62,000 plants. This is a scale comparison, not a prescription for your apartment. The underlying experiments used small, sealed chambers, where slow pollutant removal can become measurable over hours or days. Research review

Address the headaches first. Carbon monoxide is odorless and can cause headaches, dizziness and nausea. Check that you have a working CO alarm, especially if the building has fuel-burning heating, water heaters or an attached garage. If an alarm sounds, or you suspect CO exposure while having symptoms, leave immediately and contact emergency services from outside. Recurring headaches associated with the apartment deserve medical attention even if an alarm stays silent. CDC guidance
For improving the air, I would proceed in this order:

on.li: Ask the landlord to investigate ventilation and combustion appliances promptly. Your description suggests inadequate air exchange may be contributing, although it cannot identify the cause. Ask whether the apartment receives outdoor air and whether kitchen and bathroom exhausts work properly. Ventilate with clean outdoor air when conditions permit. EPA identifies source control and ventilation as the main ways to improve indoor air quality. EPA guidance

Use a properly sized HEPA cleaner if dust is a concern. Look for a published clean air delivery rate, or CADR. EPA’s sizing rule is a smoke CADR of at least two-thirds of the room’s area in square feet. For one open 670-square-foot space, that means about 450 cubic feet per minute, assuming an eight-foot ceiling. Separate rooms may need separate units. Check noise at the speed you will actually use; advertised CADR usually reflects maximum speed. Avoid ozone-generating cleaners. EPA sizing guidance, air-cleaner guide

Match gas filtration to an identified problem. HEPA filters capture particles; they do not remove formaldehyde, CO or accumulated CO₂. Substantial gas-filter media can remove some gases, but ordinary activated carbon performs poorly against formaldehyde. A thin carbon sheet is insufficient evidence that a purifier will solve your symptoms. EPA technical review

on.p: The flooring and ceiling deserve two qualifications:

on.li: Laminate can emit formaldehyde, but its presence doesn’t establish harmful exposure. Five weeks without improvement also doesn’t rule out continuing emissions. Emissions generally decline over time, while indoor concentrations depend on ventilation, temperature and humidity. Persistent symptoms justify professional assessment and targeted testing. EPA laminate guidance

Older popcorn ceilings can contain asbestos. Leave an intact ceiling alone. If it is crumbling or shedding material, ask for professional assessment before anyone scrapes, brushes or samples it. EPA asbestos guidance

on.p: Get the plants you want for enjoyment. Budget for ventilation assessment and, if dust is present, a suitably sized HEPA cleaner to address the air-quality problem.

off.p: Both excess suds and a partial drain restriction are plausible. The key distinction is whether liquid water rises in the standpipe, or only foam escapes. The late-cycle timing alone won’t distinguish them.
I’d check these possibilities:

off.li: Excess sudsing despite the “same routine.” A new bottle may have a different concentration, the measuring cap may have changed, or the water may now be softer. Soap retained in towels and other fabrics can also build up over time. Splashless bleach is another possible source of foam. Whirlpool’s suds guidance, GE’s guidance on retained detergent

A developing restriction in the trap or laundry branch. Reduced drain capacity could explain why an unchanged installation has only recently started overflowing. A main-line restriction becomes more likely if other fixtures also drain slowly or react during washer discharge. GE identifies rising water in the standpipe during spin as evidence of a household drain problem. GE troubleshooting

Drain-hose position. Check whether it has slipped farther into the standpipe, and verify insertion depth against that washer’s installation instructions. Keep the connection open around the hose; don’t seal it to contain the foam. Whirlpool installation troubleshooting

off.p: My first diagnostic would be to watch a full pump-out, then repeat with an empty washer and no detergent. Residual detergent may require more than one rinse before that becomes a useful comparison.

If liquid backs up during the detergent-free discharge, investigate drain capacity and restrictions. Test at the washer’s actual discharge rate—a small bucket or low-flow hose test can miss a marginal drain. GE lists approximately 10–17 GPM for its washers, depending on type and discharge height. GE drain-flow information

If water stays down and only foam climbs out, I’d start with detergent dosage, concentration, additives, and water hardness. My working hypothesis for the late appearance is that foam accumulates during discharge and becomes visible near the end; that’s a possibility, not proof of either a blockage or a detergent problem.

on.p: Both excess suds and a partial drain restriction are plausible. The most useful distinction is whether liquid water rises in the standpipe along with the foam. The late-cycle timing alone won’t identify the cause.
Six months of the same routine can still lead to a new problem:

on.li: A restriction develops gradually. Lint and residue can reduce capacity in the trap or laundry branch until the washer’s discharge overwhelms it. Other fixtures backing up would make a shared downstream restriction more likely.

The same detergent dose produces more foam. Check whether she opened a new bottle with a different concentration, changed bleach, or had a water softener serviced. Whirlpool identifies excess detergent, non-HE detergent in an HE washer, very soft water, and splashless bleach as possible causes of excessive suds. Whirlpool troubleshooting guidance.
Detergent residue accumulates. GE notes that suds remaining near the end of a wash cycle can indicate detergent buildup in clothing. GE residue guidance.

on.p: On the service call, I’d proceed this way:

on.li: Watch a discharge. Rising liquid and slow recession point toward inadequate drain capacity. Foam emerging while liquid stays down points more strongly toward oversudsing; both problems can coexist.

Run an empty rinse/drain with no additives. Residual detergent may require several rinses. Once the discharge is clear, repeat at the washer’s actual pumping rate. A low-flow garden-hose test can miss a restriction.
Check the hose position against the washer’s manual. Excessive insertion is a recognized installation issue. GE installation troubleshooting.
If clear-water discharge backs up, investigate the trap and branch, then the shared drain according to what the other fixtures show.

on.p: My starting hypothesis would be excess suds if it’s strictly foam, and a developing restriction if the water level also climbs.

off.p: A battery-powered leak-sensor kit with an internet-connected hub is the simplest inexpensive solution. Put a sensor under each suspect fixture; the hub sends an alert to your phone when one gets wet.
Two options worth comparing:

table: $44 for a gateway and three sensors
App notifications and email. Make sure you buy the gateway bundle.
$59 for a SpeakerHub and two sensors
Push, email, and SMS; check current SMS allowances before relying on texts.

off.p: Those prices are manufacturer listings and may vary by region or promotion. Sources: Govee kit, YoLink starter kits, YoLink notifications.
For your sinks and refrigerator, I’d start with the Govee gateway bundle for cost. To make whichever system you choose dependable over time:

off.li: Place sensors where water will collect first, below supply connections and valves. A sensing cable can cover more area behind a refrigerator.
Test the complete alert path: wet the contacts as instructed, with your phone on cellular data, and confirm the notification arrives.
Enable low-battery alerts where available, and repeat the wet test every few months.
Keep audible alarms enabled, and configure phone notifications so you’ll hear them.

off.p: Remote notification depends on a working connection. A small UPS for the hub, router, and modem can help during power cuts, but an internet outage still prevents cloud alerts. YoLink explicitly documents this limitation. YoLink FAQ

Given your previous whole-house flood, I would also consider automatic water shutoff as a later upgrade. An alert only helps if someone can respond quickly; a valve can stop the leak while you’re away. Certain YoLink sensor/controller combinations can be paired to shut the valve locally without internet, provided they’re configured correctly. YoLink leak protection

on.p: Battery-powered leak sensors linked to an internet-connected hub are a good fit for this. Place one at each likely leak location; the hub sends alerts to your phone.

For a concrete, inexpensive option, I’d consider YoLink’s hub plus four Water Leak Sensor 1 units. Its US store currently lists the kit at $69.99, with extra sensors at $16.99 each. Prices and availability vary by country. YoLink store
The features relevant to your situation are:

on.li: Free app push notifications. SMS has a limited free monthly allowance; additional messages require a paid plan. Notification details
Replaceable AAA batteries, with a manufacturer-rated life of five-plus years. Treat that as an estimate and check batteries periodically. Sensor datasheet

Detection of dripping and pooling water. Sensor 1 has no built-in audible alarm, so keep your existing beeping alarms alongside it. For awkward spaces behind appliances, Sensor 2 offers a sensing cable. Sensor comparison

on.p: Placement and testing matter as much as the brand:

on.li: Put sensors where escaping water will collect: beneath sink connections, beside toilet supply valves, and below the refrigerator’s water connection. Water must reach the sensor to trigger it.
Test every sensor with water in its intended location, then dry it. Confirm you receive an alert while your phone uses cellular data.
Enable notification sounds and any available low-battery/offline alerts. Repeat the water test periodically.

on.p: Remote alerts depend on power, your home internet connection, and the provider’s service. YoLink explicitly requires an internet connection for app functionality. A small UPS for the hub, router, and modem can cover brief power cuts; an internet outage still interrupts remote alerts. Hub requirements

Given your previous upstairs flood, an automatic water shutoff is also worth considering as a later upgrade. A notification gives you time to respond; a properly installed shutoff can stop the supply while you’re away.

off.p: Yes—small grease traps exist and can be installed on a home’s kitchen drain, subject to local plumbing and septic requirements. Search for *compact hydromechanical grease interceptors*. They often use the same designs sold for commercial kitchens, just in smaller sizes: for example, Zurn’s GT2700-04 is rated for 4 gallons per minute and holds 8 pounds of grease. That illustrates the available size; it isn’t necessarily the right size for your sink. Zurn catalog

A properly sized interceptor could reduce grease reaching your pipes and septic tank. It separates and retains grease so you can remove it. The tradeoff is another maintenance chore: you must regularly open and clean it, and neglected units can clog or smell. Installation needs suitable flow control, venting, and access for cleaning. Have a plumber select the size and confirm local requirements. Manufacturer installation guidance
For your recurring blockage, I would take these steps:

off.li: Keep as much grease out of the sink as possible. Collect cooking fat and oil separately, scrape dishes, and wipe greasy pans before washing. A grease trap supplements those habits. EPA advises against putting fats, oils, or grease down septic drains. EPA septic guidance

Have the recurring blockage location inspected before buying a trap. Grease may be the material blocking the pipe, while a sag, poor slope, rough old pipe, or a tank inlet problem helps it accumulate. A plumber or septic contractor can assess that; a camera inspection after cleaning may help. A new trap will not remove deposits already in the line.

Reconsider the monthly bacteria additive. Normal septic systems already contain the bacteria they need. EPA says additives are generally unnecessary and some can impair operation; they are not a reliable remedy for grease buildup. EPA additives fact sheet

off.p: So, a compact interceptor is a reasonable option to discuss with your plumber, but twice-yearly clogs in an old system warrant checking the pipe and tank inlet as well as controlling kitchen grease.

on.p: Yes—compact grease traps, also called grease interceptors, are available and can be installed on a home’s kitchen drain, subject to local plumbing requirements. Many are marketed for commercial kitchens, but small models exist. For example, Zurn’s GT2700-4 is rated for 4 gallons per minute and holds 8 pounds of grease. That is an example of an available size; a plumber should size yours for the sink’s discharge. Zurn specification sheet

A correctly sized, installed and maintained interceptor can reduce the kitchen grease reaching your pipes and septic tank. It needs to sit upstream of the section that clogs, with proper venting, flow control and access for cleaning. It will not remove existing deposits. Zurn installation guidance

The tradeoff is maintenance: you must regularly remove the trapped grease and solids. Cleaning frequency depends on the unit’s capacity and how much grease enters it. Once its grease capacity is exceeded, grease can pass downstream again. Schier owner’s manual
For your situation, I would take these steps:

on.li: Have a plumber or septic professional identify the exact blockage location and inspect the old system. Twice-yearly recurrence warrants checking whether pipe condition or drainage problems also contribute.
Reduce grease entering the sink. Collect cooking fats for disposal and wipe greasy pans and dishes with paper towels before washing. Texas environmental agency guidance
Ask about a small interceptor once the blockage is diagnosed. Have the plumber confirm sizing, installation requirements and cleaning access before buying one.

on.p: Also, EPA recommends against routine bacterial or chemical septic additives: the system already contains microorganisms, and additives can be ineffective or harmful. Your monthly additive should not be relied on to prevent grease clogs. EPA septic guidance

off.p: Use a water hardness test kit, available from hardware stores, aquarium shops, or water-treatment suppliers. A drop-count titration kit gives a more precise reading than test strips and is useful for checking a softener.
To check yours:

off.li: Take a sample from a cold-water tap supplied by the softener. Run the tap briefly first to clear standing water.
Test it according to the kit’s instructions.
Compare it with water taken before the softener or from a tap you know bypasses it. Outdoor taps sometimes do.

off.p: Hardness is usually reported as ppm (mg/L) as calcium carbonate or grains per gallon. One grain per US gallon equals about 17.1 ppm.

A working ion-exchange softener should produce water with very little measurable hardness. If the softened sample is nearly as hard as the untreated sample, check the salt supply, bypass valve, and regeneration settings.

A TDS meter won’t tell you the hardness: it measures dissolved substances generally, and a softener exchanges calcium and magnesium for sodium or potassium rather than removing all dissolved minerals. Existing calcium deposits also won’t disappear just because the softener is working again.

on.p: Use a total water hardness test kit. Test strips give a quick reading; a drop-count titration kit gives a numerical result by counting drops until the sample changes colour. Choose one that measures both calcium and magnesium. Hach’s hardness testing guide explains the method.
To check your softener:

on.li: Test cold water from a point before the softener, such as an outdoor tap you know receives untreated water.
Test cold water from a tap supplied by the softener. Run it long enough to flush water sitting in the pipe.
Compare the readings. A working salt-based softener should produce very low hardness. Similar readings suggest it is bypassed or needs attention.
Repeat after a regeneration cycle. If hardness falls and then returns before the next cycle, check the capacity and regeneration settings.

on.p: Kits usually report hardness as ppm or mg/L as calcium carbonate, or grains per gallon (gpg). One gpg equals approximately 17.1 mg/L. Hach
For context, the USGS hardness ranges are:
An electronic TDS meter does not measure hardness: it measures dissolved substances collectively. Use a hardness-specific test to assess the softener.

off.p: The key is to keep most of the backing on and stick the vinyl down progressively, so only a narrow strip of adhesive is exposed at a time. But first, address the bare plywood.

Sign vinyl needs a smooth, clean, nonporous surface. Sand the shelf, remove the dust, and seal it with a suitable smooth finish. Let that finish fully cure before applying the vinyl. Bare wood can give poor adhesion, and its texture will show through a gloss sheet. ORAFOL’s surface-preparation guidance specifically recommends a properly cured, smooth coating rather than porous primer.
For a plain rectangular sheet, try this:

off.li: Cut it slightly oversize. Leaving a little overhang lets you trim afterward instead of having to align every edge perfectly.
Position it with the backing still attached. Lay the shelf flat and tape one short edge of the sheet to the shelf with masking tape, making a hinge.
Fold the sheet back over the hinge. Peel back just a few centimetres of backing at that end and fold the backing sharply underneath.
Squeegee down that exposed strip. Hold the remaining vinyl clear of the surface, gently taut without stretching it. Use a clean, felt-edged vinyl squeegee to protect the gloss.

Continue a few centimetres at a time. Pull the backing out underneath, then squeegee the newly exposed strip with firm, overlapping strokes from the middle toward the sides. Keep the loose sheet off the shelf until the squeegee reaches it.
Press down the edges and trim the excess. A helper holding the loose sheet makes a large piece much easier.

off.p: This is the “hinge method”; Avery Dennison’s illustrated application guide shows the technique. That term should also help you find relevant videos.

If a wrinkle starts, stop and gently lift the freshly applied section back to where it is flat, then reapply. Pressing a wrinkle down turns it into a crease. An isolated air bubble can usually be vented with a fine pin and pressed toward the puncture, although a speck of dust underneath requires lifting and cleaning.

Wet application can make some vinyl easier to position, but don’t use it on bare plywood, and check whether your particular film permits it. For your shelf, surface preparation and controlled backing removal are the best starting points.

on.p: Use a masking-tape hinge and peel the backing a little at a time. Prepare the plywood first: sign vinyl needs a smooth, clean, nonporous surface. Sand and remove the dust, then apply a suitable gloss or semi-gloss coating and let it fully cure according to its instructions. Bare plywood’s texture can show through the vinyl and impair adhesion. ORAFOL’s surface-preparation advice
For the application:

on.li: Lay the shelf flat. Cut the vinyl slightly oversize so you can trim it after applying.

Position it with all the backing attached. Tape it temporarily in place, then run masking tape along one entire edge, bridging the vinyl and shelf. This forms a hinge that preserves your alignment. On a long, narrow shelf, hinging a short edge gives you a manageable width to work across.
Flip the sheet back on the hinge. Peel back a small section of backing nearest the hinge and fold the backing underneath.
Hold the loose vinyl slightly above the shelf. Keep it gently taut; avoid stretching it. A helper makes this easier on a large sheet.

Squeegee from the hinge outward, using firm, overlapping strokes from the middle toward each side. Advance across the exposed section gradually. The squeegee should control where the adhesive first touches the shelf.
Pull out another small section of backing and repeat. Keep the backing close behind the area you are applying.
Remove the hinge tape, press down the edges and trim the excess.

on.p: Avery Dennison’s illustrated guide, pages 4–5 shows this method. For videos, search “vinyl dry application hinge method” or “vinyl peel and squeegee application.”

Use a clean, felt-edged vinyl squeegee to protect the gloss. If a wrinkle starts, stop and gently lift the affected area while it can still release, then apply it again. For an isolated trapped bubble, a fine needle hole lets you press the air out; a folded crease needs lifting and reapplication.

Avoid wet application on bare plywood. Water-and-detergent application is an option only when the particular vinyl permits it and the surface is smooth and nonporous. ORAFOL’s wet-application guidance

off.p: A loose electrical connection is the concerning possibility here, though the two dead outlets could simply be downstream of a tripped GFCI. The symptoms alone can’t establish whether these are one problem or two.
Possible causes include:

off.li: A tripped GFCI: One outlet with TEST/RESET buttons can cut power to other outlets downstream without tripping a panel breaker. Check nearby kitchen GFCIs, including any hidden behind appliances. CPSC’s GFCI guide
A breaker that has tripped but looks on: If you can identify the affected breaker and the panel appears normal, move its handle fully OFF, then ON once. If it trips again, leave it off. CPSC guidance

A loose or failed connection: A connection at a receptacle, splice, breaker, or incoming service can interrupt power without drawing enough current to trip a breaker. Unexplained flickering warrants an electrician’s inspection. ESFI’s warning signs

off.p: Because you’re also seeing flickering in several locations, contact your utility promptly and report “partial power and intermittent flickering after storms.” Have a licensed electrician inspect the house wiring if the utility finds its supply sound. Utilities specifically recognize partial power and flickering as voltage problems to report. PG&E guidance

A loose service neutral is one possibility—particularly if some lights become unusually bright while others dim. That needs urgent attention because it can expose appliances to abnormal voltage. Don’t open the panel or remove outlets to investigate.

The microwave clock resetting while the stove clock didn’t is inconclusive: they may be on different circuits or tolerate brief interruptions differently. Increased AC use could reveal a weak connection, but doesn’t establish the cause.

If you notice burning smells, buzzing, heat, sparks, or pronounced brightening/dimming, stop using the affected equipment and seek urgent help. Smoke or fire calls for evacuation and emergency services.

on.p: A loose electrical connection is a serious possibility, and the flickering in several rooms warrants prompt attention. The symptoms alone cannot pinpoint the fault. ESFI recommends having a licensed electrician inspect unexplained flickering lights. ESFI guidance
Possible causes include:

on.li: A tripped or failed GFCI outlet. One GFCI—the kind with TEST and RESET buttons—can supply several outlets. It could explain the two dead kitchen outlets while the panel breaker remains on. Leviton guidance

A loose or damaged connection feeding those outlets. An intermittent connection could also explain flickering if the affected lights share that wiring. A breaker remaining on does not establish that the wiring is safe.

A problem with the incoming electrical supply, including a loose neutral or a failing supply connection. This becomes more concerning when several circuits are affected, particularly if some lights become unusually bright while others dim.

on.p: You can check the accessible GFCIs with no testing equipment: unplug appliances from the dead outlets, look for a GFCI supplying them, and press RESET once. If it will not reset or trips again, leave it alone and have it checked. A GFCI that refuses to reset may have lost its incoming power. Leviton troubleshooting

Also, some breakers trip into a middle position that is easy to miss. If you can identify the kitchen breaker and the panel has no signs of damage, reset it once by moving its handle fully OFF, then ON. If it trips again, leave it off. Keep the panel cover in place. Schneider Electric instructions

Contact your utility to report the partial outage and flickering, and arrange an electrician promptly. Utilities treat this combination as a potential supply problem. Even if a GFCI reset restores the outlets, recurring flickering still needs investigation. DTE outage guidance

If lights become markedly brighter or dimmer, stop using appliances and call the utility urgently. Burning smells, crackling, hot outlets, or sparks require immediate attention; smoke or fire warrants evacuation and emergency services.

The storms may be relevant, but the clocks cannot establish the cause. Different appliances can retain their time through different lengths of interruption. The stove keeping its time does not rule out an outage or a supply fault.

off.p: In normal, steady operation, air at the vent should not be 10–15°F colder than the air leaving the evaporator coil. Your doubt about those readings is reasonable, but the discrepancy alone doesn’t establish which contractor’s diagnosis is correct.

The evaporator removes heat. After that, ordinary ducts provide no further refrigeration; air usually gains heat on its way to the rooms, especially through ducts in a warm attic. DOE’s duct guidance describes this heat gain.
Several things could explain the reported numbers:

off.li: Different kinds of measurements. An infrared “temperature gun” measures surfaces, not the air flowing past them. A reading aimed at a register or air-handler cabinet therefore isn’t directly comparable to an air-probe reading. Surface material and reflected infrared radiation can also affect the result. FLIR explains how infrared thermometers measure temperature.

Different parts of the airflow. Air immediately downstream of a coil may not be uniformly mixed. One probe could sample a warmer stream while a duct branch receives colder air. The air hasn’t become colder along that branch; the measurements sampled different streams.

Different times or locations. Cycling, insufficient time for the thermometer to settle, or a probe touching warm metal can distort the comparison. Also, “above the coil” means downstream only if the air flows upward.

off.p: A dry register surrounded by warmer room air cannot, at steady state, be colder than all the air cooling it without some additional cooling mechanism. Evaporation from a wet register or a register still cold from an earlier operating condition are possible exceptions. The pressure drop through an ordinary residential vent cannot explain a 10–15°F reduction.

The useful next step is to have the technician compare air temperatures with suitable probes, during the same continuous cooling run, at the coil’s downstream side and inside the supply register, keeping the probes off metal. Sampling several positions downstream of the coil would check for uneven temperatures.
Neither “55°F at the handler” nor “low 40s at the vent” alone proves the system is healthy. Those readings need context, including entering-air temperature, humidity, and airflow.
This fits a home-improvement/HVAC question well; moving it to Physics SE isn’t necessary.

on.p: A drop from 55°F after the evaporator to the low 40s at a vent would be very unusual in an ordinary residential A/C system. If those are accurate measurements of the same airstream during steady operation, something would have to remove additional heat along the way.
Supply air generally warms as it passes through ducts surrounded by warmer rooms or attic air. Heat passes through the duct walls; insulation reduces that transfer. DOE duct guidance.
Several things could explain the reported readings:

on.li: Surface temperature versus air temperature. If the inspector used an infrared thermometer, it measured the grille or a surface inside the duct. Shiny metal can also produce misleading readings because it reflects infrared radiation and has low emissivity. Fluke’s measurement guidance.
Different parts of the airflow. Temperature immediately after a coil can vary across the duct. A probe reading 55°F in one spot may miss a colder stream feeding a particular branch.

Different operating conditions or probe placement. Measurements taken at different times, before the probes settle, or with a probe touching metal can give an unreliable comparison. “Above the coil” also needs to mean downstream in the actual airflow direction.

on.p: A dry grille cooled only by the passing air cannot remain colder than that air at steady state. Additional cooling could come from evaporation on a wet grille or contact with something colder. Likewise, ducts surrounded by air colder than the supply could cool it further. Those would require specific evidence in your installation.

The useful next step is to have the temperatures repeated with air probes, during the same continuous cooling run, downstream of the coil and inside the vent’s airstream. Take several readings across the supply duct.
These two numbers alone establish neither normal operation nor a system fault. Evaluating performance also requires return-air temperature, humidity, and airflow.
This is a practical HVAC troubleshooting question; Home Improvement SE is an appropriate place for it.

off.p: A faint stain can stay; actual glue residue needs to be removed or sealed before you skim coat. You don’t need to scrape until the drywall looks spotless, especially if that starts damaging its paper facing.

Check a stubborn spot with a damp sponge: if it becomes slippery, sticky, or gummy, there’s still adhesive there. Moisture from the joint compound can soften that adhesive and compromise the skim coat’s bond.
For your situation:

off.li: Remove the remaining loose glue and any raised deposits.
Wipe with clean water to remove the vinegar and dissolved paste, then let the wall dry thoroughly.

Apply a sealer specifically rated for wallpaper adhesive residue, such as Zinsser Gardz, and let it dry according to the label before skim coating. The manufacturer explicitly states that it seals old wallpaper paste and helps prevent bubbling when damaged drywall is coated with joint compound. Manufacturer guidance

off.p: With only faint, firmly attached traces remaining, sealing first is a reasonable way to proceed.

on.p: Yes—faint, firmly attached residue can remain if you seal it before applying the skim coat. Remove any raised glue deposits and loose material first. Zinsser’s Gardz technical sheet specifically allows residual wallpaper adhesive after thicker deposits have been removed.

A faint stain alone doesn’t tell you whether glue remains. Dampen a small spot: if it becomes slippery or gummy, keep cleaning that area gently. Avoid scraping so aggressively that you tear the drywall paper.
For your next steps:

on.li: Wipe the wall with clean water to remove loosened glue and cleaning solution, then let it dry thoroughly.
Apply a sealer specifically rated for wallpaper adhesive residue, such as Gardz, across the wall.
Let the sealer dry according to its label, then skim coat.
After the mud dries, sand and prime before painting.

on.p: Sealing matters because moisture can reactivate leftover paste and cause cracking or peeling. Gardz is also rated for joint compound applied over it. Manufacturer guidance.

off.p: Yes—this can often be reduced with a local repair, without replacing all the ductwork. Your explanation is plausible: sheet metal expands as it warms and contracts as it cools. If it catches against framing or a tight support, it can release suddenly with a “ping.” Some ticking is common; how the ducts are supported helps explain why one house is noisier than another. This Old House’s heating expert describes this mechanism and possible fixes.
Start with these steps:

off.li: Check the filter and vents. Replace a dirty filter with the type specified for your system, open closed supply registers, and make sure return grilles aren’t blocked by furniture. Airflow restrictions can make flat duct panels flex and pop—called *oil-canning*. A Canadian HVAC contractor explains these causes.

Note exactly when it happens. Pings as the ducts warm up or cool down suggest thermal movement. A pop immediately when the blower starts or stops suggests pressure-induced flexing. This distinction helps identify the repair.

Locate it before changing anything. During a quiet heating cycle, listen along accessible basement ductwork, particularly near supports and places where ducts pass through framing. Record the noise and mark the suspected location for a technician.

off.p: For thermal movement, the repair may be adjusting a hanger or providing clearance and suitable isolation padding where the duct rubs against wood. For a flexing rectangular panel, a sheet-metal technician can add reinforcement or repair that section, while also checking for excessive duct pressure. Insulation can sometimes reduce transmitted sound, but I’d locate the source before paying to wrap the ducts. Repair guidance, panel reinforcement guidance.

Ask an HVAC contractor who does sheet-metal duct repairs for a “duct noise diagnosis and localized repair.” Tell them you want the source located, supports/contact points inspected, and airflow/static pressure checked. That is a reasonable service call; wholesale replacement is not the starting point. Access may be the main complication if the offending section is behind a finished ceiling.

on.p: Your explanation is plausible: sheet-metal ducts expand as they warm and contract as they cool. If a duct rubs against framing, that movement can produce a sharp ping. Another cause is a flat duct panel flexing as air pressure changes, called “oil-canning.” Some expansion noise is common; its loudness depends on how the ducts are fitted and supported. Heating expert Richard Trethewey explains both causes here.
Start with a few simple checks:

on.li: Note when it happens. Pings during warming and cooling suggest thermal movement. A pop exactly when the blower starts or stops suggests pressure-related flexing. These are clues to guide an inspection.
Check the furnace filter and replace it if dirty, using the type specified for your system. Keep return grilles clear of furniture.
Open any supply registers you’ve deliberately closed. Closing registers to quiet a room can create airflow and pressure problems. Carrier explains that restriction here.

Listen near accessible ductwork through a heating cycle. Look for a duct touching a joist or a broad panel visibly snapping inward or outward. Record the sound and timing to help a technician reproduce it. Restore’s diagnostic guidance recommends these observations.

on.p: Yes, you can hire someone for a targeted repair. Ask an HVAC contractor who does sheet-metal ductwork for a “duct popping/noise diagnosis.” Ask them to reproduce the noise, locate the moving section, and check static pressure if it coincides with blower operation.

Depending on the cause, a local fix might involve adjusting a support, adding suitable isolation pads where the duct contacts wood, or reinforcing a panel that flexes. These are repairs worth investigating before considering extensive replacement. Trethewey recommends isolating contact points; Restore describes support, reinforcement, and airflow checks.
I’d start with the filter/register checks and locating the sound. Leave blower-speed changes and duct reshaping to the technician, since the repair needs to preserve the furnace’s required airflow.

off.p: Yes—this is usually possible, provided the wiring and ceiling box are suitable. A 120 V, 6 A opener can generally use a 15 A circuit, but the other loads on that circuit and the opener’s installation instructions also matter.

For an ordinary single-pole switch, the conversion typically involves replacing the ceiling lampholder with a properly mounted 15 A grounded receptacle, and connecting the switch’s supply and switched-hot conductors together with a listed connector. The former switch box must remain accessible with a blank cover. The actual connections depend on whether power enters at the ceiling or the switch, so identify the wiring first; a white wire in an older switch loop can be a hot conductor.
A few conditions matter:

off.li: Grounding: The new receptacle needs a proper equipment-grounding path, which may be a grounding wire or suitable metal raceway. GFCI protection does not create a ground, and neutral must never be jumpered to the grounding terminal. Leviton grounding guidance

GFCI protection: Modern NEC editions require it for garage receptacles, including ceiling outlets for openers. Your existing upstream GFCI can provide this protection if the light connection is actually downstream of it. Garage GFCI requirements

Garage lighting: If this is your only wall-controlled garage light, removing it creates a code issue. NEC 210.70 requires a wall-controlled lighting outlet in a garage with electricity; do not assume the opener’s built-in light satisfies that requirement. Garage lighting requirements

off.p: The preferable arrangement is to retain the switched light and add an always-powered receptacle near the opener. If constant power already reaches the ceiling box, that may be straightforward; otherwise, additional cable may be needed.

Turn off the breaker and verify the wiring is de-energized before working. Have an electrician identify the circuit arrangement if you cannot confidently distinguish the conductors, and confirm local permit requirements—the applicable code depends on your jurisdiction.

on.p: Yes, this is usually possible, provided the wiring has a suitable hot, neutral, and equipment ground, and the circuit has enough capacity.

An electrician can replace the ceiling lampholder with a grounded receptacle and reconnect the switched feed for constant power. If the switch is removed, any splices must remain inside its electrical box with an accessible blank cover. The actual connections depend on how the existing light and switch are wired; wire colors alone are insufficient to identify them.
There are three important conditions:

on.li: Keep the required garage lighting. Garages generally require a wall-controlled lighting outlet. If this is your only garage light, replacing it and removing its switch would eliminate that required lighting. Adding an unswitched receptacle alongside the existing light is usually the practical solution. County electrical guidelines

Preserve GFCI protection and grounding. Verify that the new receptacle actually receives protection from your existing GFCI. Its test/reset device should be readily accessible, such as at a wall receptacle or the breaker panel. GFCI protection does not supply a missing equipment ground. Leviton’s code explanation

Check the entire circuit load. A 6A opener can generally operate on a 15A circuit, but other connected equipment and motor starting current matter. Modern NEC editions require a 20A circuit for the required garage convenience receptacles while permitting additional 15A circuits for other receptacles. Your locally adopted code determines how alterations to the existing installation are handled. Leviton’s garage circuit guidance

on.p: Have an electrician inspect both boxes and add a permanently powered, grounded receptacle while retaining the switched light. Check local permit requirements and the opener’s installation instructions. Before any wiring work, shut off the breaker and verify that the conductors are de-energized.

off.p: Choose angular crushed stone over rounded gravel. If the “uniform gravel” means pea gravel or smooth river gravel, the 5/8-inch minus is better for stability and leveling: its angular pieces interlock, and the smaller particles fill gaps so it compacts firmly.
There is a drainage tradeoff:

off.li: 5/8-inch minus: compacts into a firm, easily leveled base, but its fines reduce drainage.
Clean crushed stone, roughly 3/4 inch: provides good support and better drainage around wooden skids. This is the material recommended by shed-foundation installer Site Prep.

off.p: For a typical skid-supported shed, I’d favor clean angular crushed stone, especially on a damp site. Whichever you choose, remove sod and topsoil, place it on firm ground, compact it, and keep the finished pad above the surrounding grade so water can escape. Good preparation matters more than the difference between those two crushed-stone products.

on.p: For stability and leveling, 5/8-minus crushed stone is a good choice on a well-drained site. Its angular pieces interlock, and the smaller particles fill gaps so it compacts into a firm base.
The distinction is the stone’s shape and grading:

on.li: Rounded gravel, such as pea gravel, shifts under load and is a poor choice beneath skids.
5/8-minus crushed stone compacts tightly but drains more slowly because it contains fines.
Clean angular crushed stone, commonly 3/4-inch, drains well and also supports shed skids. Shed-foundation contractor Site Prep recommends this material.

on.p: For a typical small shed, remove sod and organic topsoil down to firm ground, then install roughly 4–6 inches of stone, compacted in thin layers. Keep the finished pad above surrounding grade, provide an outlet for water, and support the skids evenly along their length. Soft or wet soil may require additional preparation. South West Butler Quarry’s guidance supports that depth and the choice between clean stone for drainage and minus stone for greater firmness.

I can’t see the “like this” example, so if your uniform gravel is angular clean stone, it’s a viable option too. For wood skids where drainage matters most, I’d favor clean crushed stone; for your stated priority of firm leveling on dry ground, I’d use the 5/8-minus.

off.p: No—don’t rely solely on moisture from the ground. It may eventually harden some of the mix, but you can’t count on enough water reaching all of it evenly, leaving weak or powdery areas.

The “dry” method is often misunderstood: Quikrete Fast-Setting Concrete can be poured dry into the hole, but you then add water. That is the manufacturer’s recommended method; “no mixing” does not mean “no water.” Follow the water quantity and placement instructions on your particular bag. Quikrete’s post-setting instructions
Also check which product you have. Quikrete is a brand with several mixes; ordinary concrete mix should be mixed with water before placement unless its instructions specifically allow otherwise.
For wood posts, use lumber rated for ground contact and shape any exposed concrete to shed water away from the post.

on.p: Add water. Relying on ground moisture is an unreliable way to set a fence post. Soil moisture varies, so you cannot count on it to wet the entire mix and produce a sound footing.

QUIKRETE’s Fast-Setting Concrete Mix can be poured dry into the hole, but its instructions then call for about 1 gallon of water per 50-pound bag, allowing the water to saturate the mix. They specify waiting about four hours before building the fence or loading the post. QUIKRETE’s post-setting instructions
Check your exact bag: QUIKRETE sells several mixes, and the dry-pour method applies to its Fast-Setting product. Follow the water and mixing directions for whichever product you have.

For wood posts, use wood rated for ground contact. QUIKRETE also recommends a compacted gravel base and sloping the concrete surface away from the post to help manage moisture. QUIKRETE’s wood-post guidance

off.p: Your concern is justified: a premixed skim coat cannot be relied on to protect an unsuitable cement–sand base plaster from cracking. However, site-mixed plaster is not automatically unsuitable for AAC.
AAC needs a compatible render because:

off.li: Dry blocks can absorb mixing water too quickly, impairing the plaster’s curing and adhesion.
Cement-rich plaster can shrink excessively, causing cracks or separation from the blocks.
Movement at openings, concrete-frame junctions and movement joints needs appropriate detailing; additives alone cannot accommodate it.

off.p: Hebel’s technical guidance explicitly allows site-mixed render, but warns against strong, cement-rich mixes and calls for compatible strength, adhesion and vapour permeability. It also specifies mesh at vulnerable locations and warns against rendering across movement joints. Hebel technical manual, pp. 9.1–9.3

Polymer modification helps, but it is not a guarantee against cracking. Suitable additives can improve adhesion, toughness and flexibility. Site-mixed polymer-modified render is possible—for example, Sika supplies SBR additives for renders—but a generic additive recipe is not proof that the resulting mix suits your particular AAC. Get an AAC-approved specification covering proportions, preparation, thickness and curing. Sika’s render-additive guidance

Your skim coat primarily provides a smooth finishing surface. Some products can cover minor surface cracks, but that is different from preventing future cracks in the underlying plaster. My practical assessment is that cracks may reappear through the skim, and a skim cannot rescue a base coat that loses adhesion. Weber’s guidance treats skim coating as a finishing step alongside correct mixing and curing. Weber Thailand guidance

If plastering has not started, I would spend the extra money on an AAC-approved base render unless your block supplier can provide a proven site-mixed alternative. The base coat is where compatibility matters most. In tropical conditions, protect fresh render from direct sun, wind and heavy rain, and follow the specified curing procedure. Sika application instructions
If it is already applied, assess its bond and any cracking before skimming; ordinary plaster does not necessarily need removal simply because it was mixed on site.
What country are you building in, what is the skim-coat product, and are these interior or exterior walls? Those details would help determine whether your proposed combination is suitable.

on.p: Your concern is justified: the base plaster’s compatibility with AAC matters, and a skim coat cannot reliably compensate for a base that cracks or loses its bond. If you have yet to apply the plaster, I would choose a base render explicitly approved for your AAC blocks.
AAC creates several challenges for plaster:

on.li: High suction: the blocks can draw water out of fresh plaster, affecting curing and adhesion. Surface preparation and suction control matter.
Shrinkage: a cement-rich render can shrink enough to crack or separate from the AAC. Hebel’s technical manual specifically warns against strong, cement-rich mixes for this reason.
Movement: joints and transitions between AAC and concrete can concentrate stress. These need appropriate detailing.

on.p: Hebel’s technical guidance discusses shrinkage and separation; its application guidance includes suction control in hot weather.

Polymer modification can improve adhesion and toughness and reduce cracking, depending on the formulation. A suitable AAC render also needs compatible strength, controlled shrinkage and, outdoors, appropriate water resistance and vapour permeability. “Polymer-modified” and “pre-mixed” alone do not establish suitability. For example, Hebel’s PowerBlock guide expressly excludes general-purpose sand/cement renders, including bagged products, for those blocks. Your own block manufacturer’s specification should govern your choice.

Your skim coat primarily smooths the surface. My assessment is that cracks in the base may transmit through it, and a detached base can carry the skim coat with it. Treat crack-bridging capability as something that must be stated in the product’s technical data.
For your project, I would:

on.li: Get the AAC supplier’s approved plaster specification. A site-mixed render may be acceptable if they provide a formulation and application procedure for it.
Check the skim coat’s data sheet for permitted substrates, interior/exterior use, thickness and waiting time over fresh render.

Follow the specified preparation, mesh and curing procedure. Tropical sun and wind make protection during curing particularly relevant. Movement joints must continue through the finish; mesh does not replace them. Hebel’s guide covers both mesh and movement joints.

on.p: A manufacturer-specified additive could be a cheaper route to an acceptable site mix, but adding SBR or acrylic latex to an arbitrary mortar recipe does not establish AAC compatibility. Sika’s SBR guidance describes its benefits for renders; the complete mix still needs approval for your substrate.

What country are you building in, what are the AAC and skim-coat brands, and are these interior or exterior walls? Also, has the cement/sand plaster already been applied? Those details would let me assess your proposed combination more specifically.

off.p: It should stay in place if left undisturbed, but I would cover it in the storage area you describe. Safe’n’Sound is a fairly firm, friction-fit mineral-wool batt; ROCKWOOL says it holds between studs without sagging. It shouldn’t simply crumble from age in a dry interior wall. Manufacturer’s product information

That doesn’t make it a durable wall surface. My practical expectation is that repeated scraping, box corners, and pressure against it would tear or compress the batts and loosen fibers. Occasional light contact is different from using it as the surface behind stored boxes.

Pegboard attached to the studs would provide useful protection. However, for reducing furnace noise in the family room, solid drywall on both sides would perform better: the insulation absorbs sound within the cavity, while the solid wall faces provide the sound barrier. Pegboard’s holes limit that benefit. You could leave the furnace-side drywall untaped and unpainted if appearance is your main objection.

One qualification: Safe’n’Sound itself is noncombustible, but that does not make an open stud wall a fire-rated separation. Before choosing pegboard, check whether your local requirements call for a particular furnace-room wall assembly, and maintain the furnace and flue clearances. ROCKWOOL’s published fire and sound ratings apply to complete assemblies that include drywall. ROCKWOOL assembly examples

on.p: For the storage-room use you describe, I’d cover it with pegboard. Safe’n’Sound is firm enough to friction-fit between studs and stay in place. ROCKWOOL says its insulation retains its properties over the building’s lifetime, assuming it avoids physical damage. Sitting undisturbed should cause little deterioration; repeated rubbing, snagging, and pressure from boxes can damage the exposed surface. Product information, manufacturer FAQ.

Pegboard screwed to the studs would provide useful protection against bumps. It still leaves openings through which dust or fibers can escape, so handle the batts carefully and avoid compressing them behind the board.

For sound isolation, drywall on both sides with sealed edges would perform better than the open or pegboard-covered arrangement. You could leave the furnace-room drywall untaped and unpainted if appearance is your main objection, although sealing joints helps reduce sound leakage.

Before choosing pegboard, check whether your local rules require a fire-rated furnace-room partition. Noncombustible insulation alone does not establish a wall’s fire rating; the complete wall assembly matters. Also preserve the furnace’s specified clearances and combustion-air supply when enclosing the room. ROCKWOOL’s guidance on rated assemblies, DOE combustion-equipment guidance.

off.p: It’s worth checking, but 21 amps alone doesn’t mean your compressor is failing. That’s about 19% above 17.6 amps.

If the label says RLA (Rated Load Amps), that’s a reference rating used for electrical sizing—not necessarily the compressor’s maximum allowable running current. Actual current depends on operating conditions and the specific compressor. Copeland explains RLA here.
Two details matter:

off.li: Startup or steady running? A brief startup surge is expected. A steady 21-amp reading after several minutes deserves further evaluation.
Compressor alone or entire outdoor unit? A reading on the unit’s incoming power includes the condenser fan, so it isn’t directly comparable to the compressor’s RLA.

off.p: If it’s consistently drawing 21 amps on the compressor alone, have an HVAC technician check operating voltage, capacitor, condenser airflow, refrigerant pressures, and the manufacturer’s expected current for those conditions. A dirty condenser can increase compressor energy use. Carrier’s guidance
Turn it off if it trips the breaker repeatedly, struggles to start, smells burned, or the outdoor fan stops while the compressor runs. Avoid probing inside the powered electrical compartment.
Was the 21 amps measured during startup or while running steadily—and on a compressor wire or the unit’s incoming supply?

on.p: A steady 21-amp reading deserves checking, but those two numbers alone don’t establish a problem. It’s about 19% above the tag’s 17.6 amps.

Assuming “RL” means RLA—rated load amps, that value is used for electrical component sizing. The compressor’s allowable maximum continuous current can be higher; the exact limit depends on its model. Copeland’s explanation of compressor current ratings.
The measurement matters:

on.li: During startup: A brief current surge is expected.
While running steadily: Have an HVAC technician compare the reading with the manufacturer’s specifications and check operating voltage, condenser airflow, and refrigerant pressures.
Measured at the outdoor unit’s supply: The reading includes the fan’s current, which affects comparison with the compressor tag.

on.p: Turn it off and arrange service if it trips the breaker, repeatedly shuts down, smells burned, or hums while failing to start. Avoid further checks inside the energized electrical compartment; capacitors can retain a charge after power is disconnected. Copeland’s safety guidance.
Was the 21 amps measured during steady operation, and was it measured on a compressor wire or the whole unit’s supply? What’s the compressor’s make and model?

off.p: Choose a ballast by its approved lamp combinations, supply voltage, and wiring requirements. Matching physical size or total wattage alone is insufficient.
The easiest replacement is the same model as the original, or a manufacturer-approved equivalent—provided the fixture still uses the intended lamps.

off.li: Read the tube markings. Record the complete lamp designation, such as F32T8, F40T12, or F54T5/HO. Length and diameter alone do not establish compatibility; standard-output and high-output tubes can require different ballasts. Lamp color codes such as “830” or “841” generally do not affect ballast selection.

Count the lamps operated by each ballast. A four-tube fixture might contain two two-lamp ballasts. The replacement must explicitly support your lamp type and the number of lamps you will connect. A ballast advertised for “one or two lamps” can support either configuration, using its specified wiring diagram. Manufacturer selection tools, such as Fulham’s lamp and wiring-diagram finder, identify the approved combinations.

Match the electrical supply. Check input voltage and frequency against the fixture’s supply. “Universal voltage” means the stated range, such as 120–277 V; it does not mean every voltage worldwide. Do not confuse input voltage with the ballast’s lamp-output voltage.

Check wiring and lamp holders. The new ballast may have a different wiring diagram or different numbers of wires. Follow its diagram rather than reconnecting by wire color alone. Lamp holders—often called *tombstones*—may be shunted, meaning their two contacts are electrically joined, or non-shunted. Rapid-start and programmed-start systems generally require separate connections to both lamp pins; a change in starting method may therefore require new holders or rewiring.
Check fit and operating conditions. Confirm case dimensions, mounting holes, permitted mounting arrangement, temperature ratings, and any special requirements for dimming or emergency lighting.

off.p: For an upgrade while retaining fluorescent tubes, compare these features:

table: A compatible electronic model can replace an older magnetic ballast, usually reducing hum and visible flicker. Conversion may require rewiring.
Instant start suits lamps left on for long periods. Programmed start preheats the electrodes and is usually preferable for frequent switching or occupancy sensors.
Indicates relative lamp light output. Match the old value for similar brightness; a higher value generally increases brightness and power consumption. It is different from *power factor*.
Must suit the lowest expected temperature, especially in garages or outdoor fixtures.
Requires a ballast compatible with the particular control system. Ordinary ballasts are not automatically dimmable.

off.p: Manufacturers list lamp combinations, ballast factor, and starting-temperature limits separately; compare those specifications rather than relying on “latest” or “high efficiency” in a product description. Example manufacturer specification sheet.
If you want LED tubes, choose the conversion approach before buying a ballast:

off.li: Type A: Runs from a ballast; the exact ballast must appear on the LED tube manufacturer’s compatibility list.
Type B: Bypasses the ballast and requires rewiring according to the LED tube’s instructions.
Type C: Uses a separate LED driver.

off.p: These distinctions are explained in LEDVANCE’s LED tube guide.

Before opening or rewiring the fixture, isolate power at the breaker and verify it is de-energized. Have a qualified electrician handle the replacement if you cannot safely verify the supply or interpret the wiring diagram.
To identify a specific replacement, provide the old ballast’s model number, the tube markings, the lamp count per ballast, and the supply voltage.

on.p: Choose a ballast that explicitly supports your exact tube type, the number of tubes it will operate, and your fixture’s supply voltage. The old ballast’s model number is a useful starting point; confirm a replacement against its manufacturer’s lamp table and wiring diagram.

Before opening the ballast compartment, disconnect power at the breaker or unplug the fixture, and verify that it is de-energized. Use an electrician if you cannot safely identify and test the wiring. Manufacturer safety instructions
Record these details:

table: Read the printing on the tube—for example, F32T8 or F40T12. Match the complete lamp designation, including any HO/high-output designation. Matching length alone is insufficient.
Count the tubes connected to each ballast. A four-tube fixture may contain two ballasts. The replacement must list your intended lamp count.
Match the actual electrical supply to the ballast’s input rating. “Universal voltage” covers only the range printed on that product.
Check case dimensions, mounting holes, available space, and lead lengths.
Check the replacement’s wiring diagram and socket requirements. Wire count and colors can differ from the old ballast.
Check minimum starting temperature, particularly for garages or outdoor fixtures, and compatibility with any dimming or emergency equipment.

on.p: Manufacturers provide selection tables organized by lamp type, wattage, and quantity. For example, Fulham’s selection tool supplies the corresponding wiring diagram; Advance’s ballast catalog lists lamp and input-voltage combinations.
For an upgrade, choose an electronic fluorescent ballast approved for your lamps. Then consider:

on.li: Starting method: Programmed-start ballasts preheat the lamp electrodes and suit frequent switching, including occupancy-sensor use. Instant-start ballasts suit lamps that remain on for extended periods. Changing starting methods may require rewiring or replacing lampholders; programmed-start models commonly require non-shunted sockets, whose two contacts are electrically separate. Advance starting guidance, Fulham socket requirements

Brightness and energy use: Compare the manufacturer’s system light output and input watts for your lamp combination. Ballasts are offered with different ballast factors, so compatible replacements can produce different brightness. Advance product options

on.p: Follow the new ballast’s wiring diagram. A T12-to-T8 conversion requires a ballast approved for the new T8 lamps and compatible fixture components. Similar-looking tubes can have different electrical requirements.

If your goal is an LED upgrade, select the LED system first. Ballast-compatible tubes require a ballast on the lamp manufacturer’s compatibility list; ballast-bypass tubes require the specified fixture rewiring. LEDVANCE retrofit guidance
For a specific replacement, provide the tube designation, old ballast model or label photo, tube count, and your country or supply voltage.

off.p: Your sand may absorb some water, but much of the “thirst” is probably the extra paste needed to make the grains move past one another. Dryness, fineness, and the amount of sand all matter.

First, 0.42 is not a universally optimal water:cement ratio. That number is associated with theoretical water requirements for complete cement hydration under particular conditions; it does not guarantee a workable mortar. Use ratios by mass, and choose the mix around both its hardened properties and its ability to be placed and consolidated. ACI curing guide
Several effects explain what you’re seeing:

off.li: Dry sand really can absorb water into pores within its grains. Mix designs normally account for this using *saturated surface-dry* sand: its internal pores are full, but there is no excess water on the grain surfaces. Sand drier than that requires additional absorption water; wetter sand contributes water to the batch. Water added to satisfy absorption is treated differently from extra free mixing water when calculating the effective water:cement ratio. ACI moisture corrections

Fine sand increases water demand even if it absorbs very little. It has more surface area to wet and lubricate. Grain shape and size distribution also affect packing and friction. Your fine paint-texturing sand performing worst fits this explanation, although its actual composition is unknown. Mortar grading study

You may have too little cement paste for the amount of sand. A water:cement ratio specifies the composition of the paste, but says nothing about how much paste surrounds the aggregate. Too little paste leaves a harsh, gritty mix. A superplasticizer can make the paste flow better, but cannot supply missing paste volume. American Cement Association

off.p: For scale, suppose you use 1 kg cement, 3 kg completely dry sand, and 420 g water. If that particular sand has 1% absorption, it needs approximately 30 g additional water to reach its saturated surface-dry condition. That is an illustrative calculation, not an assumed absorption value for your sand.

Hand mixing can contribute, particularly with a stiff mix and a PCE that needs thorough distribution. But it need not be the main cause. Also, “0.5% by weight” needs a denominator: admixture dosages are commonly based on cement or total cementitious material, and liquid products and powders have different concentrations. Follow your particular product’s instructions for dose, addition sequence, and mixing time. For example, one Sika PCE specifies thorough wet mixing for at least 60 seconds in a mixer; that does not translate directly into 60 seconds of hand stirring. Sika product instructions

Clay contamination is another possible reason for poor PCE response, especially with backyard sand. Certain clays adsorb the admixture and greatly reduce its effectiveness. Sieving alone does not establish that sand is clean. PCE–clay research
For your next small trial:

off.li: Use clean, washed sand intended for mortar or concrete, with a range of grain sizes.
Weigh everything and record the sand:cement ratio as well as water:cement.
Try presoaked sand, drained and brought approximately to surface-dry condition. Simply draining it can leave surface water, so this is a diagnostic trial rather than precise moisture control.
Use the PCE exactly as its instructions specify, mixing small batches thoroughly before deciding more water is necessary.
If it remains gritty, test a lower sand:cement ratio while keeping water:cement fixed.

off.p: Yes, other people’s damp sand can supply water that your desert-dry sand lacks. Hot, dry conditions can also increase evaporation and accelerate workability loss, so mix in shade with cool materials and protect the finished material during curing. NRMCA hot-weather guidance
A pourable, self-consolidating mixture needs a suitable overall formulation. Holding water:cement at 0.42 and adding PCE to an arbitrary mortar recipe does not necessarily produce one.

on.p: Your sand probably causes both water absorption and a higher demand for cement paste. Desert dryness can contribute, and hand mixing can make the problem harder to overcome.

First, 0.42 is not a universally optimal water:cement ratio. It is a plausible target for some mixes, measured by mass, but the right ratio depends on the required strength, durability, workability, and ingredients. The American Cement Association recommends lowering it as far as practical while retaining enough workability for proper placement and consolidation. ACA guidance
There are two distinct effects behind the “thirst”:

on.li: Absorption: Dry sand can take water into pores within its grains. Mix calculations normally account for this using the *saturated surface-dry* condition, or SSD: the internal pores are full, and the grain surfaces carry no extra water. Water needed to bring dry aggregate to SSD is excluded from the effective water:cement ratio. Wet sand’s surface water counts toward that ratio. NRMCA moisture guidance

Paste demand: Cement paste must fill the spaces between grains and provide enough coating for them to move past one another. Adding sand while holding cement and water constant leaves progressively less paste available. Fine sand has more surface area per kilogram; angular grains and poor grading also increase demand. This produces exactly the harsh, gritty consistency you describe. FHWA guidance

on.p: The very fine texture sand performing worst is consistent with increased surface area. Its actual composition and suitability for cement mixtures would need checking.

For an illustrative calculation, suppose you use 1 kg cement and 3 kg completely dry sand with a measured absorption of 1%. The sand needs 30 g water to reach SSD. You would then add 450 g total water to supply 420 g effective mixing water and maintain an effective ratio of 0.42. That 1% is an example; your sand’s absorption must be established. Simply soaking and draining sand leaves an uncertain amount of surface water.

Your PCE result also needs a little investigation. “0.5%” alone does not establish whether the dose is suitable: the product’s concentration, whether it is liquid or powder, and the specified dosing basis matter. Addition sequence and thorough mixing matter too. For example, one Sika PCE specifies 0.8–1.0% of cementitious mass for ordinary workability, higher doses for flowing concrete, and at least 90 seconds of wet mixing. Those instructions apply to that product; follow yours. Sika product instructions
Backyard sand could also contain clay. Some clays adsorb PCE strongly, reducing the amount available to disperse cement. Sieving does little to remove clay coating the grains. Experimental study
For your next small trial:

on.li: Use clean, washed sand intended for the mixture, with a suitable range of grain sizes.
Weigh everything and account for aggregate moisture.
Follow the PCE’s dosing and addition instructions. Mix thoroughly, scraping and folding the whole batch before judging its consistency.
If it remains gritty, test a lower sand:cement ratio while keeping the effective water:cement ratio fixed. Improvement would point toward insufficient paste.
Mix in shade and protect the placed material during curing. Low humidity, heat, and wind increase moisture loss. NRMCA hot-weather guidance

on.p: A pourable, self-consolidating mix needs a deliberately balanced paste volume, aggregate grading, and admixture system. NRMCA SCC guidance
What cement:sand proportions are you using, by mass, and what is the exact PCE product? Those details would help distinguish absorption, insufficient paste, and admixture problems.

off.p: Possibly, but one episode of humming doesn’t prove the motor is failing. Humming usually means the motor has power but isn’t turning; a jam can cause that and trip the overload reset. Moen’s troubleshooting instructions describe this symptom.

A plausible explanation is that your Allen-key work freed the obstruction, but the motor was still too hot to restart reliably. InSinkErator says its overload protector may need up to 20 minutes to cool. That could explain why it worked the next morning. InSinkErator reset guidance
The useful distinction is whether the shaft turned freely after you worked it loose:

off.li: If it was stiff or caught at particular points, suspect debris or mechanical binding. With the recent cabinet work, construction debris is worth checking for.
If it turned freely through full revolutions but still hummed, an intermittent motor starting fault becomes more likely. Cooling alone wouldn’t explain continued humming while the shaft was free.

off.p: If it happens again, switch it off promptly and disconnect power before checking it; don’t leave it humming or put your hand inside. If it repeatedly refuses to start despite turning freely, replacement is a reasonable choice for a 20-year-old disposal. Its successful restart is encouraging, but doesn’t rule out an intermittent fault.

on.p: It could be developing a motor problem, but one episode of humming doesn’t establish that. Humming usually means the motor has power but cannot start turning.

A plausible explanation is that you freed a jam with the Allen key, while the motor was still hot from the stalled attempts. The popped reset button supports an overload event. InSinkErator’s troubleshooting guidance calls for freeing the shaft and allowing the motor to cool before restarting. Manufacturer guidance
The useful distinction is what happened after your reset:

on.li: It went silent: overheating and the overload protector could explain the delay.
It continued humming while the shaft turned freely: cooling alone is a less complete explanation. An intermittent motor starting fault becomes more plausible.

on.p: Since this followed cabinet work, check for debris that could have entered the disposal. Disconnect power first, use a flashlight and tongs, and keep your hands out of the grinding chamber.

If it now starts promptly and runs normally, monitor it. If it hums again, switch it off immediately. Repeated humming with a freely turning shaft warrants inspection; at approximately 20 years old, replacement would be a reasonable choice if an internal motor fault is confirmed.

off.p: Based on your description, I would not accept this as a completed drainage repair. If the concrete actually covers the bottom 2 inches of your vinyl siding and remains level, there are two concerns:

off.li: The siding is buried. Vinyl siding needs clearance above the slab so it can move and drain. For reference, the 2024 International Residential Code specifies at least ½ inch clearance above slabs, unless the manufacturer or another code provision specifies otherwise. Concrete overlapping the siding is a red flag. Your local code and the siding manufacturer’s instructions determine the applicable requirement. ICC wall-covering requirements

The drainage problem may remain. A rain-exposed porch should generally slope away from the house—typically 2%, roughly ¼ inch per foot. A truly level slab does not provide that drainage. U.S. Department of Energy guidance

off.p: Ask the builder in writing for a correction that addresses the slab elevation, slope, siding clearance, and flashing where the porch meets the wall. Simply caulking the joint would not address the lack of slope.

Take dated photos of the overlap and video of any pooling during rain. Then contact your local building inspector to review the work; an independent inspector with experience investigating water intrusion can also check the wall connection and any damage from the earlier leakage.

A slight slope can look flat, so have it measured—but the reported siding overlap still needs review. What state or country is the house in, and can you share a photo of where the concrete meets the siding?

on.p: Based on your description, I would not accept this as a completed drainage repair. Concrete covering the bottom 2 inches of vinyl siding, combined with a porch that still has no slope away from the house, warrants an inspection.
There are two concerns:

on.li: Drainage: A flat slab can leave water pooling against the house. As a U.S. benchmark, the 2024 International Residential Code generally requires paved surfaces within 10 feet of the foundation to slope away at least 2%—approximately ¼ inch per foot. Your local building department can confirm the applicable requirements and any landing exceptions. IRC drainage requirements

The siding connection: Vinyl siding needs room to move and a path for water behind it to drain. Concrete poured against and over it may obstruct both. The wall also needs properly integrated flashing and a water-resistive barrier to protect the materials behind the siding. Exact clearance depends on the siding manufacturer’s instructions. Vinyl Siding Institute installation manual

on.p: Notify the builder in writing now, with photos showing the concrete overlap and any pooling after rain. Request a written repair plan addressing both drainage and the slab-to-wall connection. Ask your local building inspector to examine the work; an independent inspector experienced with water intrusion can also help.

The repair may require lowering or replacing the slab and correcting the siding and flashing. An on-site inspection should determine that. A bead of caulk alone would not correct the flat slab’s drainage.
What state or country is the home in, and was the concrete poured directly against the vinyl?

off.p: Yes—PVC can be located, but an ordinary metal detector will not detect the pipe itself.
