For a 100 mm waste drain, there are two useful approaches:

off.li: Drain camera with a locating transmitter (“sonde”). Feed it into the drain through an accessible cleanout, then use a matching handheld receiver outside the wall to locate the camera head. Moving the head and marking successive positions traces the pipe’s route. Ask a plumber for a *drain camera inspection with sonde locating*. RIDGID explains locating PVC this way.

Radar wall scanner rated for empty plastic pipes. Some professional scanners can detect these through a wall, subject to wall construction and detection depth. Check the specifications carefully: models that detect only water-filled plastic pipes may miss a waste drain, which is normally mostly empty. Bosch lists these capabilities separately.

off.p: Running water and listening along the wall can help narrow down the route, but does not establish an exact position. If you need to locate the pipe accurately before opening the wall, a sonde is usually the most practical choice when there is drain access.

on.p: Yes. For a 100 mm PVC waste pipe, two types of equipment are useful:

on.li: A drain camera or probe with a sonde: A sonde is a small transmitter pushed into the pipe through an accessible opening, such as a cleanout. A handheld receiver locates it through the wall. Moving the probe and marking successive positions lets you trace the pipe’s route. Ask a drain specialist for a “camera inspection with sonde locating.” RIDGID’s locating equipment supports this method.

A radar wall scanner rated for empty plastic pipes: Some scanners can detect these, depending on the wall construction and pipe depth. Check the specifications carefully: a scanner advertised for *water-filled plastic pipes* may be unsuitable for a waste pipe, which normally contains air. Bosch lists both capabilities for certain detectors.

on.p: An ordinary metal detector will not detect PVC itself. A basic stud finder might register a change behind plasterboard, but that reading cannot reliably identify it as a pipe.

For your drain, I would start with sonde locating if there is access into the pipe. If access is unavailable, consider a suitable radar scanner or inspect the wall cavity with a borescope through a carefully chosen opening. The wall material and depth matter as much as the pipe’s diameter.
Before drilling or cutting, confirm the position and check for nearby electrical cables; a detector reading alone does not establish that a spot is safe to drill.

off.p: This strongly suggests a loose, damaged, or disconnected main neutral—and the 50-amp breakers create a separate fire hazard. Stop using the electrical system until it is inspected.

In a normal 120/240-volt home supply, the neutral keeps both groups of 120-volt circuits at the proper voltage. When that connection fails, plugging something in can make voltage drop on one group and rise on the other. That explains why some lights dim while others become unusually bright, and why heaters behave differently depending on the outlet. Appliances can receive dangerously high voltage. This is a likely diagnosis, but an on-site inspection must confirm it. Power Monitors’ explanation
Take these steps now:

off.li: Switch off the main breaker if you can safely operate its normal handle without removing covers. If the panel is hot, buzzing, sparking, or smells burned, stay away and have the utility disconnect power.

Call your utility’s emergency/service number and a licensed electrician today. Tell them: “Lights brighten and dim when loads change; I suspect a lost neutral.” Explain the 300-foot underground aluminum run and the breaker replacements.

Have the electrician restore correctly sized breakers before power is restored. Ordinary lighting and receptacle circuits generally require 15- or 20-amp protection, depending on their wiring. A 50-amp breaker can allow those wires to overheat without tripping. Larger breakers cannot correct voltage problems. CPSC wiring-hazard guidance

off.p: The neutral fault could be at the utility connection, meter equipment, either end of your buried cable, or within the cable itself. A poor aluminum termination or damaged insulation allowing underground corrosion could explain why it worked for six months before deteriorating. Power Monitors

The electrician should also assess the cable’s capacity and voltage drop over 300 feet, and verify grounding and bonding. Leave the walls open until the wiring has been inspected. Don’t keep plugging in loads to investigate or retighten service connections yourself.

on.p: Your symptoms strongly suggest a loose or broken main neutral connection. Treat this as an urgent electrical hazard. An electrician needs to confirm the fault and locate it.

In a typical Texas home’s 120/240-volt supply, the neutral keeps each side’s outlets near 120 volts. When that connection fails, switching on a load can pull one side’s voltage down and push the other side’s voltage up. That explains lights dimming in some places, becoming unusually bright elsewhere, and heaters changing output. The excessive voltage can damage equipment and create fire and shock hazards. Explanation from a licensed electrician.
Do this now:

on.li: Stop plugging things in to test the problem. If you can safely operate the main disconnect using its normal external handle, turn the house’s power off. Leave it off until inspected. If the equipment is hot, sparking, or making crackling sounds, keep away.

Call your utility’s emergency/outage number and a licensed electrician now. Tell them: “Lights across the house get unusually bright or dim when loads turn on. I suspect a failing service or feeder neutral.” Explain that you installed the 300-foot underground feed.
Tell the electrician about every 50-amp breaker you installed. This is a separate, serious hazard that must be corrected before restoring power.

on.p: Ordinary lighting and receptacle circuits generally need 15- or 20-amp protection matched to their wiring. A 50-amp breaker can allow those wires to overheat before it trips. Increasing breaker size cannot stabilize voltage; breakers protect against excessive current. Your history of never tripping one does not establish safety. The CPSC’s home-wiring guide specifically warns that oversized breakers on lighting and outlet circuits can cause fires.

Given the widespread symptoms, the electrician should prioritize the neutral path from the utility supply through the meter, underground cable, and house panel. A deteriorated termination or damaged buried conductor could explain why the problem appeared after six months; inspection is needed to establish the cause.

Also have them evaluate the 300-foot cable’s sizing, burial suitability, and grounding arrangement. If “4-4-2” describes three conductors, they need to establish whether your installation requires a separate equipment-grounding conductor. Keep the walls open until the wiring and breaker corrections have been inspected.
If you see smoke or fire, leave and call 911.

off.p: The strongest reasons are preventing tipping and keeping the countertop’s supports fixed and level. Your plumbing and caulking concerns are additional benefits.

off.li: Tipping: Loaded drawers move weight forward when opened. Someone leaning on an open drawer—or a child climbing it—adds an overturning force. A heavy cabinet may feel stable during ordinary use without being stable under those conditions. IKEA explicitly requires anchoring its base cabinets for safety. IKEA guidance

Alignment and support: Installers shim cabinets level, fasten neighboring cabinets together, and secure them in position. That establishes a stable support for the countertop and keeps doors and drawers aligned. KraftMaid specifies this installation sequence. KraftMaid installation guide

Connected parts: A typical continuous countertop ties several cabinets together. Moving one cabinet can strain countertop joints, disturb its support, or pull on sink connections. Larger plumbing holes provide clearance, but don’t make the connections movable.

off.p: The wall is simply a convenient anchoring point. Islands demonstrate that wall attachment isn’t essential: KraftMaid instead requires those cabinets to be secured to floor blocking. Installation guide

Your maintenance advantages are real for independently movable units with their own tops. A kitchen designed around freestanding furniture can provide them. Ordinary fitted cabinetry, however, is designed to work as a fixed assembly; leaving out the wall screws alone doesn’t give it the stability or independence of freestanding furniture.

on.p: The strongest reasons are preventing tipping and keeping the countertop’s supports fixed in position.

on.li: An open drawer changes the balance. A loaded drawer puts weight ahead of the cabinet; someone leaning on it or a child climbing it adds more overturning force. Wall screws resist that force. How significant this is depends on the cabinet’s weight, depth, and connections to adjacent units. IKEA explicitly requires its base cabinets to be secured to the wall for safety.

A continuous countertop needs stable support. Cabinets are leveled and often shimmed individually, then fastened together and to the wall. Moving one can disturb that support, stress countertop joints, or cause cracking around cutouts in brittle tops. Cambria requires supporting cabinets to be structurally sound, straight, level, and square.

Anchoring preserves the installation’s alignment. Repeated drawer pulls, bumps, and leaning against the counter can move a loose unit. Screws keep appliance gaps, cabinet fronts, and wall joints where they were set.

on.p: Your cleaning, painting, and flooring advantages are real for independently movable units with their own tops. A conventional cabinet run usually has a shared countertop and cabinet-to-cabinet fasteners, so removing the wall screws alone won’t make one cabinet movable. A sink unit also needs its plumbing disconnected before substantial movement; generous access holes only provide clearance around the pipes.

Freestanding kitchen furniture can work when designed for that use. For ordinary fitted cabinets, a few removable screws provide dependable restraint at little installation cost. Plumbing clearance and caulk are secondary reasons.

off.p: Yes—generally, you can remount it 4–5 inches lower on the same wood studs, provided the studs are sound and the original installation didn’t split or damage them. Two existing screw holes per stud ordinarily won’t meaningfully weaken the stud or the grip of new screws several inches away.

With your mounting holes about 8 inches apart, lowering the bracket 4–5 inches would put each new hole at least about 3–4 inches from the nearest old hole. That should leave plenty of intact wood between them for a typical TV mount.
When reinstalling:

off.li: Locate the stud centers again at the new height.
Follow your mount’s instructions for screw size, pilot-hole diameter, and drilling depth.

Tighten the screws firmly without overtightening or stripping the wood. Manufacturer instructions emphasize these points because improper installation can reduce holding strength. Example SANUS installation instructions
If a screw spins without tightening, or you find evidence of a split, stop and have that attachment checked.

off.p: You can patch the old drywall holes cosmetically; they don’t need filling to restore holding strength at the new locations. Being on the first floor of a two-story house doesn’t, by itself, change this answer.

on.p: Yes—generally, you can remount it 4–5 inches lower on the same sound wood studs. The new screws will grip fresh wood. A few small, separated holes ordinarily have little effect on the studs’ structural strength, including in a first-floor load-bearing wall.

With your existing holes about 8 inches apart, lowering the bracket 4–5 inches would put the closest new hole roughly 3–4 inches from an old hole. That is generally ample separation for typical TV-mount lag screws, assuming the wood hasn’t split.
For the remount:

on.li: Remove the TV with someone’s help before loosening the bracket.
Confirm each stud’s center at the new mounting height.
Follow your mount’s instructions for screw size, pilot-hole diameter and depth. Use 7/32 inch again only if that is the specified size.
Tighten the screws until the bracket is firmly seated. Overtightening can strip the wood and reduce holding strength; Sanus’s installation guidance gives the same caution.

on.p: If a screw spins without tightening, or you find cracked or deteriorated wood, have the attachment checked before hanging the TV. You can patch the old drywall holes cosmetically; filling them isn’t needed to support the new mounting location.

off.p: You’re correct: in a correctly wired, healthy circuit, opening just the live wire stops current through both the appliance and its neutral wire. A single-pole switch is therefore sufficient for ordinary on/off control, and is widely used.
The advantage of a double-pole switch is disconnecting the appliance from both supply conductors, which matters when something is wrong:

off.li: Live and neutral are reversed: A single-pole switch may then open the actual neutral. The appliance stops working, but its internal wiring remains connected to live. Touching it while grounded can complete a new circuit through your body. A double-pole switch disconnects both wires regardless of their orientation.

Neutral becomes hazardous: Neutral is normally close to earth potential, but wiring faults—such as a broken upstream neutral—can raise its voltage. Opening only live leaves the appliance connected to that neutral. Electrical Safety First’s isolation guidance discusses circumstances in which neutral can become live.

off.p: The key distinction is that “no current is flowing” does not mean “no dangerous voltage is present.” Current needs a complete path; touching a connected conductor can create that path.

So a single-pole switch can be used where ordinary switching is sufficient. A double-pole switch provides more complete disconnection where isolation is required. For maintenance, the device must also be suitable for isolation, and the circuit must be verified dead before work. HSE guidance

on.p: Your reasoning is correct: opening the live wire stops the normal load current in both live and neutral. A single-pole switch is therefore sufficient for ordinary on/off control in a correctly wired circuit.

The advantage of double-pole switching is disconnecting the appliance from both supply conductors. This matters because a wire can carry no current and still have a dangerous voltage relative to earth.
Two situations explain the benefit:

on.li: Live and neutral are reversed. A single-pole switch could then open the actual neutral. The appliance stops operating, but its internal wiring remains connected to live. Touching that wiring while grounded can complete a circuit through your body. A double-pole switch opens both conductors.

The neutral develops a dangerous voltage. Neutral is normally close to earth potential, but supply faults or wiring errors can raise its voltage. Opening both conductors also disconnects the appliance from that neutral. Electrical Safety First specifically cautions about working on neutral conductors where single-pole isolation is used. Safe isolation guidance

on.p: So a single-pole switch can serve as an operating switch; a suitable double-pole isolator provides more complete disconnection for safety. Whether single-pole isolation is permitted depends on the supply arrangement and applicable electrical rules.
Before working on equipment, the supply must be safely isolated and the relevant conductors proved dead—even with a double-pole device. HSE safe working guidance

off.p: Yes—there are more compact options, but the grounds still need a reliable connection. Assuming you’re in the U.S. and installing cable with a proper equipment-grounding conductor:

off.li: Use a listed grounding crimp sleeve. It takes less room than a wire nut. Use the specified crimping tool and wire combination; ordinary pliers aren’t sufficient.

Use a green grounding wire nut with a pass-through hole. One ground wire can extend through the connector to the receptacle’s green screw, saving a separate pigtail. These options are shown in IDEAL’s grounding connector catalog.

With a properly grounded metal box, use a listed self-grounding receptacle. This can eliminate the receptacle pigtail. The metal box still needs its own approved grounding connection, and the mounting must meet the self-grounding device’s requirements. See Leviton’s grounding guidance.

off.p: Don’t put multiple wires under a screw unless it’s rated for them, or use the receptacle as the connection that maintains ground continuity downstream. Removing the receptacle must leave the other grounds connected.

Check the box’s permitted fill before choosing a connector. Physically squeezing everything in doesn’t establish that the box is large enough. If it’s undersized, a compatible listed extension ring with marked additional volume can add space outward without requiring a deeper wall cavity. Hubbell makes extension rings for additional box capacity.
Turn off the circuit and verify it’s de-energized before working. Never connect the receptacle’s ground terminal to neutral.

on.p: Yes—a listed crimp connector can make the ground splice more compact, and a self-grounding receptacle can eliminate the separate wire to the receptacle in a properly grounded metal box.
Assuming you’re in the U.S. and installing new cable with an equipment grounding conductor:

on.li: Crimp sleeve: Use a listed connector approved for your grounding wires’ size, material, and number. Leave a conductor extending from the splice for the ground connection. Use the manufacturer’s specified crimping tool; ordinary pliers won’t produce the required crimp. IDEAL’s crimp instructions

Feed-through grounding connector: A green grounding connector with a hole in its end lets one longer ground wire extend through the splice to a grounding terminal, saving a separate pigtail conductor. Follow its wire-combination instructions. IDEAL grounding connectors

Self-grounding receptacle: With a metal box, bond the box to the incoming grounds using an approved grounding screw or listed clip. A receptacle specifically listed as self-grounding can then ground through its mounting connection, subject to its installation requirements. Ground continuity to downstream outlets must remain intact when the receptacle is removed. Leviton’s grounding guidance

on.p: Check box fill before choosing a connector. A compact splice helps physically, but the box still needs enough calculated volume for the wiring, receptacle, and internal clamps. If it’s too small, a compatible extension ring with marked volume can add space outward from the baseboard. Hubbell’s box-fill guidance
Turn off the circuit and verify it is de-energized before working. These options require a valid grounding path back to the supply; attaching a wire to an old metal box alone does not establish one.

off.p: Close the propane tank valve after each use. Leaving it open does not automatically cause a leak if everything is working properly, but it leaves the hose, regulator, connections, and fireplace valve supplied with gas.

The fireplace’s control valve stops gas reaching the burner; it cannot stop a leak at a hose or connection upstream of it. With the tank valve open, a leak there can continue feeding propane into the surrounding area. Accumulated gas can ignite and cause a fire or explosion. Closing the tank valve limits that supply. Weber’s gas shutoff guidance

For a propane fire pit, follow your model’s shutdown instructions and close both valves when finished. For example, American Fyre Designs explicitly requires closing the cylinder valve after every use. Fire pit owner’s manual

If reaching the valve requires lifting the whole fireplace, check its manual for the intended access method—there may be a removable panel or a particular tank orientation. Ask the manufacturer about an approved arrangement that makes the valve accessible. Also confirm that your added firestones are approved for that model and placed as instructed.

If you smell gas or hear hissing, stop using it. Close the tank valve only if safe, move away, avoid flames and electrical switches, and call the fire department or propane supplier from a safe location. Propane safety guidance

on.p: Close the propane tank valve after each use. Relying on the fireplace control alone leaves the hose, regulator and connections supplied with gas. Manufacturers recommend shutting off the fuel supply when a portable gas appliance is idle. Weber safety guidance

An open tank valve does not automatically cause a leak: an intact system with its burner valve closed should stop gas flow. The risk is that a damaged hose, loose connection or faulty valve can release gas continuously while the tank remains open. Propane is heavier than air and can collect near the ground or inside a poorly ventilated enclosure. A spark or flame can then cause a fire or explosion. Closing the tank valve cuts off the supply to those downstream components. Propane Education & Research Council safety guide
For your setup:

on.li: Check the manual’s tank-access instructions. If you must lift the whole fireplace to reach the valve, ask the manufacturer how it is intended to be accessed. Avoid lifting or tilting a burning or hot appliance.
Keep the tank compartment’s ventilation openings clear, and use the specified tank position.
Use only the firestones approved for your model, in the amount and arrangement its manual specifies. Rock placement can affect burner operation. Example fire-pit installation instructions

on.p: If you smell gas or hear hissing, do not light the fireplace. Move everyone away, avoid flames and electrical switches, and call the fire department or propane supplier from a safe location. PERC emergency guidance
What brand and model did you buy? That would let me check the intended valve access and shutdown procedure.

off.p: Let the filter dry before reinstalling it, and ideally keep a spare so you can run the system while it dries.

off.li: Running without a filter for three hours: A single short period is unlikely to cause immediate damage in an ordinary, relatively clean home, but I wouldn’t make it a monthly practice. Unfiltered dust can accumulate on the blower and indoor coil. Leave the system off while the filter dries, or install a clean spare. Filters protect the equipment as well as improve air quality. Carrier’s filter guidance

Reinstalling a wet filter: Unless your particular filter’s instructions explicitly allow it, let it dry completely. Shaking removes loose water but may leave moisture in the material. Three hours isn’t a universal requirement—drying time depends on the filter, temperature and humidity. Trane’s general guidance says to dry reusable filters completely before returning them to service. Trane’s cleaning instructions

Using a disposable replacement: Generally yes, provided your air handler permits it, it fits securely without gaps, and its airflow resistance is suitable for the system. Don’t automatically choose the highest MERV rating; check the equipment manual or have your technician confirm compatibility. Carrier’s filter-selection guidance

off.p: For the 15 × 21 × 1 size, distinguish the filter’s measured dimensions from its advertised “nominal” size. Give an HVAC supplier the actual measurements and air-handler model number to identify a compatible replacement. A second matching washable filter is also a straightforward solution: swap them each month and let the washed one dry at leisure.

on.p: Let the filter dry completely, and keep the system off while it dries—or install a suitable dry spare.

on.li: Running for three hours without a filter: A single short period is unlikely to cause immediate damage in an ordinarily clean home, but that is a general assessment, not a guarantee for your unit. Unfiltered air carries dust into the blower and indoor coil; repeated exposure can cause buildup. I would avoid making this your monthly routine. Trane explains the filter’s protective role.

Putting the filter back wet: Let it dry fully unless its manufacturer explicitly permits damp installation. Shaking removes loose water but can leave moisture in the filter. Three hours is only an estimate; drying time depends on the material, humidity, and airflow. Trane’s maintenance instructions require washable filters to be thoroughly dry before reinstallation.

Using a disposable replacement: Generally, yes, provided your air handler permits it, it fits securely, and its airflow resistance is suitable. Confirm the permitted filter type and MERV rating in your manual or with the technician. A higher filtration rating can be too restrictive for some systems. Trane’s filter guidance discusses this limitation.

on.p: For your 15 × 21 × 1 filter, check whether those are measured dimensions or the size printed on the frame. Disposable filters have both *nominal* and *actual* dimensions, which differ. Compare actual measurements before ordering; an HVAC supplier may be able to provide a custom size. Trane explains filter sizing.
A second compatible washable filter would also let you swap in a dry one immediately after cleaning.

off.p: A small steel offset mounting plate is a clean solution if you need to move the hook sideways by ½ inch. The plate screws into the stud, and the hook bolts to the plate at the offset position. Paint it to match the wall and keep it mostly hidden behind the hook.

Use two vertically spaced screws into the stud to resist rotation. The hook needs a proper metal connection—such as a tapped hole or a bolt with a recessed nut behind the plate. Choose a plate and fasteners suitable for the roll’s weight and the pull from operating it; a thin decorative mending plate may flex.

If you mean moving the backdrop ½ inch farther out from the wall, use solid ½-inch spacers behind both mounting brackets instead, with correspondingly longer screws that retain the required penetration into the studs.

Either arrangement keeps the load supported by the framing. Backdrop manufacturer ALZO’s installation guide likewise calls for securing its brackets to studs. The right plate thickness and screw sizes depend on your hooks and the loaded roll’s weight.

on.p: A small steel offset plate is a clean way to move the hook sideways by ½ inch while keeping it supported by the stud.
The arrangement would be:

on.li: Fasten the plate through the drywall into the stud, with two screws spaced vertically.
Attach the hook to a second set of holes, offset sideways by ½ inch.
Paint the plate to match the wall, or size it so the hook’s base hides most of it.

on.p: Search for “offset mounting plate” or have a metal shop make a small plate to match your hook. The hook connection needs threaded holes or clearance for a bolt and nut behind the plate; an ordinary flat mending plate may need modification.

Choose the plate thickness and screws for the combined weight of the roll and crossbar, plus the force of pulling the backdrop down. A ½-inch offset alone doesn’t establish a safe capacity: the steel, screws, and wood connection all matter. Simpson Strong-Tie’s connection guide treats steel strength and fastener capacity separately.

If you mean moving the backdrop ½ inch farther out from the wall, use a solid ½-inch spacer behind the mounting bracket, with appropriately longer screws into the stud. That solves a depth-clearance problem; the offset plate solves a sideways-clearance problem.
Also check the actual hanging position before drilling: moving a support sideways only moves the backdrop if the crossbar and roll are secured against sliding.

off.p: A hole saw is suitable—buy a 2¼-inch bi-metal hole saw rated for steel, plus its matching arbor and pilot drill. Hole saws aren’t limited to wood; manufacturers make them specifically for sheet steel. Starrett’s metal-cutting hole saws
For thin galvanized sheet:

off.li: Mark the center and make a small center-punch dimple so the pilot drill doesn’t wander.
If you can reach inside, clamp a scrap wood block tightly behind the sheet. This supports the metal and reduces vibration and snagging.
Drill with the hole saw square to the surface, at low speed, using cutting oil and steady, light pressure. Follow the saw’s recommended speed for steel.
Ease the pressure as the saw breaks through. Hold the drill firmly with both hands; the teeth can catch.
File or deburr the edge before fitting the exit seal, and protect exposed steel with a suitable touch-up coating.

off.p: Wear eye protection and check that the pilot bit and saw have clearance from anything inside the box.

Another option is a knockout punch, which makes a clean hole if you have access to both sides. Drill a starter hole, assemble the punch and die through it, and tighten the draw bolt. Buy by actual hole diameter: conduit-size labels don’t necessarily match the hole diameter. Greenlee offers a 2¼-inch actual-hole-size die. For just a couple of holes, the bi-metal hole saw is usually the more economical choice.

on.p: Use a 2¼-inch bi-metal hole saw rated for steel, with a matching arbor and pilot drill. Hole saws do cut metal; bi-metal versions are commonly used for mild-steel sheet. Starrett’s application guidance specifically covers this use.
For your box:

on.li: Check clearance inside. Make sure the pilot drill and saw cannot hit ducts, wiring, or anything else. If the panel is removable, take it down and cut it on a workbench.
Mark and center-punch the hole center. Clamp a scrap wood block tightly behind the sheet if accessible; this helps keep thin metal from flexing and catching.
Use a variable-speed drill in low gear, with hammer mode off. Apply cutting oil and follow the saw manufacturer’s speed recommendation for steel.

Hold the saw square to the panel and feed steadily. Ease the pressure as it breaks through. Hold the drill securely—the saw can catch and twist it. Starrett recommends steady, perpendicular feed and cutting oil. Cutting instructions
File or deburr the edge, collect the metal chips, and install the seal according to its instructions.

on.p: Wear eye protection, keep hands clear of the rotating saw, and work from secure footing on the roof.

Another option is a sheet-metal knockout punch, which makes a clean hole but requires access to both sides and a starter hole for its draw bolt. Check its *actual cutting diameter*: electrical punches are often labeled by conduit size. For example, Greenlee’s “2-inch” conduit punch makes a 2.416-inch hole. Greenlee specifications
For a few holes, the bi-metal hole saw is a straightforward choice.

off.p: Install the main ductwork before the cabinets, then mount the hood and make the final duct connection after the cabinets are installed. With the cabinets out of the way, you’ll have easier access for cutting openings, fastening the duct, and sealing joints.
The best sequence is:

off.li: Choose the hood and finalize the cabinet layout. Its installation instructions determine duct size, outlet location, and clearance above the cooking surface.
Install the exterior vent and rough ductwork, positioning the hood end to match that layout. Arrange the electrical supply at this stage too.
Install the cabinets, with any necessary duct openings.
Mount and connect the hood, then finish any soffit or enclosure above the cabinets.

off.p: For the run above your cabinets, allow enough space for the duct and its elbows before deciding cabinet height or crown molding. Use the specified duct size and keep the route short and straight; those details affect hood performance. Zephyr installation guidance
Use metal ductwork and terminate it outdoors through a suitable wall or roof cap—not in the attic. Broan installation instructions

on.p: Install the main ductwork before the cabinets. With a new exterior vent and ducting above the cabinets, you’ll have better access for cutting openings, supporting the duct, and sealing joints.
The practical order is:

on.li: Choose the hood and finalize the cabinet layout. Use the hood’s installation instructions to establish duct size, outlet position, and clearance above the cooking surface.
Install the exterior vent and main duct run, leaving the final connection at the hood accessible.
Install the cabinets, with any required duct openings.
Mount the hood and complete the duct connection, then finish any enclosure or trim.

on.p: This follows Broan-NuTone’s installation sequence, which starts with the exterior cap and metal ductwork, working back toward the hood location.

Coordinate the duct installer and cabinet installer before either starts: the duct must fit above the planned cabinet height and align with the hood. Use smooth, rigid metal duct sized for your chosen hood, with a short route and few elbows; discharge it outdoors. Broan-NuTone duct guidance

off.p: Yes—a two-part metal epoxy may secure the loose screw, but a solid support block is the simplest temporary fix.
I don’t see the GIF attached here. From your description, the threaded stud’s attachment inside the leg may have broken—possibly a weld, rather than a missing nut.

First, check the sofa’s threaded socket by trying a working leg in that position. If that leg also won’t screw in easily, the socket may be damaged; fixing the loose stud alone won’t solve it. Don’t force either leg.
If the socket is sound, you could try this repair:

off.li: Remove the faulty leg. Clean and dry the accessible metal around where the stud enters the cap, then roughen the bonding area with sandpaper.
Apply two-part metal epoxy around that junction, working some into the gap if accessible. Keep the threads that enter the sofa clean.
Hold the stud straight and at the same protruding length as a good leg while it cures.
Wait for the full cure before reinstalling. Original J-B Weld specifies 15–24 hours; follow your product’s instructions. Manufacturer’s preparation and curing guidance.

off.p: This is a possible temporary repair, with strength depending on how much sound metal the epoxy can grip. A small bead around a very wobbly stud may fail.

For immediate support, use a broad, solid wooden block of the correct height beneath the sofa’s structural frame near the failed leg. Make sure it sits flat and cannot slide or tip; avoid loose stacks of books or bricks.
For a lasting repair, replace the leg with one matching its height, thread diameter, and thread pitch, or have its stud attachment repaired by a metalworker.

on.p: A broad wooden block under the sofa’s solid frame is the simplest temporary fix. Match the height of the other legs and place it near the damaged leg’s mounting point. It must sit firmly on the floor and support solid framing; fabric or thin underside panels cannot carry the load. Avoid using the sofa if the block can rock or slide.
From your description, the stud’s attachment inside the metal leg may have broken loose. A failed weld or retaining piece could explain it; a missing nut is only one possibility.

Before trying glue, check the sofa’s socket: with the sofa securely supported, try a good leg in that location. If it screws in normally, the damaged leg is the problem. If it also fails to catch, the sofa’s threaded fitting needs attention.
Metal epoxy is a possible temporary repair if the loose stud is still securely captive inside the leg:

on.li: Pull the stud outward gently and hold it straight.
Clean and dry the accessible metal around the stud and the cap’s hole. Roughen the bonding surfaces if you have sandpaper.
Apply two-part metal epoxy where the stud enters the cap, keeping the exposed threads clean.

Hold it upright and still until fully cured. Original J-B Weld specifies a 15–24-hour cure; allow the full 24 hours before installation. Follow the product’s preparation instructions. J-B Weld instructions

on.p: That may stop the stud spinning enough to install the leg. Its strength depends on what remains attached inside, so don’t rely on glue alone if the stud can pull out or the leg still wobbles. Keep the temporary block supporting that corner.
For a lasting fix, replace the leg with one matching its height, stud diameter, and thread pitch. Taking the damaged leg to a hardware shop makes matching the thread easier.

off.p: Connecting the laundry and sinks to your septic system can be a sound solution—but only if the tank and leach field can handle the added flow. Septic systems commonly receive those wastes. Your concern is valid because your existing system has been operating with that water diverted elsewhere.

The main long-term risk is overloading the leach field. Extra water can saturate it, and large surges through the tank can carry solids into the field, contributing to clogging. A system working well under its current load does not prove it has spare capacity. EPA guidance
Here’s how I’d evaluate the options:

off.li: Connect to septic: Investigate this first. Have a qualified septic designer or inspector review the original permit, tank size, field size and condition, household occupancy, and estimated added water use. Ask whether the system was originally designed for *all* household wastewater, and why the graywater was separated. The proposed connection should route wastewater through the septic tank before the leach field.

Install a new drywell: Potentially reasonable if locally permitted and the new site has suitable soil and groundwater clearance. First confirm why the existing one stopped draining—a blocked pipe, accumulated material, and saturated surrounding soil call for different remedies. Replacing it without identifying the cause could repeat the problem.

Overflow pipe over the hill: If this means dumping untreated wastewater onto the ground, I would avoid it. Sink and laundry wastewater can carry contaminants; moving the outlet downhill does not provide treatment. An approved subsurface graywater dispersal system would be a different proposal. EPA explanation of wastewater and surface-water contamination

off.p: Before spending the $3,000 or $5,000, I’d get the septic capacity assessment and check acceptable options with your local health/environmental department. In the U.S., those authorities generally maintain permit records and regulate modifications. EPA permit and inspection guidance
If you connect to septic, spread laundry throughout the week, fix leaks, and keep grease and food scraps out of the sinks. Those measures reduce hydraulic and solids loading. EPA maintenance guidance
What state/country are you in, how old is the septic system, and do those sinks include the kitchen sink? Those details would help narrow the advice.

on.p: Connecting the washing machine and sinks to your septic system can be a sound option if the tank and leach field have capacity for the added flow. Conventional septic systems commonly handle all household wastewater. Your concern is valid because yours has been operating with some of that water diverted elsewhere. EPA’s explanation of septic systems

The main long-term concern is overloading the leach field. Added water can shorten settling time in the tank and saturate the field, potentially causing backups or sewage surfacing. Laundry creates concentrated bursts of flow; EPA recommends spreading loads throughout the week. EPA maintenance guidance
Here’s how I would assess the options:

on.li: Connect to septic: Have a qualified septic professional review the original design, inspect the system, and assess whether it can handle your combined wastewater flow. Tank size alone doesn’t establish leach-field capacity. The proposed connection should send wastewater through the septic tank before it reaches the field.

Install a new drywell: First confirm why the existing one stopped draining. Have the inlet checked for blockage and the disposal area assessed for soil clogging or groundwater problems. A replacement needs an approved location and suitable soil; another hole nearby may encounter the same conditions.

Overflow over the hill: If this means an open pipe discharging onto the ground, I would avoid committing to it until the local health department confirms the proposal is permissible. Graywater disposal has restrictions, and kitchen-sink water can receive different treatment under local rules. For example, Arizona excludes kitchen-sink water from graywater and prohibits graywater runoff off the property. Arizona graywater guidance

on.p: My next step would be a septic capacity assessment and a call to the local health department before choosing a bid. Ask the evaluator to document whether the field can accept the additional flow and whether any upgrades are needed. A cheap connection could become expensive if it overloads an aging field.
What state/country are you in, and do those sinks include the kitchen sink? Those details would help narrow the permitted options.

off.p: Favor 12" OC joists over extra rows of blocking, keeping the blocking already specified. For otherwise identical framing, closer joist spacing is the more dependable way to improve firmness.

Blocking restrains joist twisting and can help neighboring joists share a footstep load. But it does not shorten the unsupported span or increase each joist’s bending stiffness. Its benefit depends on the connections and the whole deck assembly; extra blocking alone will not reliably eliminate bounce. Research on between-joist bracing

Changing from 16" to 12" OC gives you roughly one-third more joists and shorter spans for the decking boards. Under an evenly distributed load, each identical joist carries 25% less load, so its calculated bending deflection is about 25% lower. That does not translate directly into 25% less bounce under a footstep.
For the solid feel you want, also consider:

off.li: Deeper joists. Joist bending stiffness increases approximately with the cube of their actual depth.
Shorter unsupported spans, using another properly supported beam if practical.
Stiff beams and appropriate post spacing. Flexible beams can make the whole deck bounce despite closely spaced joists.

off.p: Assuming your beam is about 12' from the house, you have roughly a 12' supported span plus a 2' cantilever. Both need checking against the selected joist size, species, grade, and local requirements; a 2' overhang is not automatically acceptable. The AWC deck guide checks the span and overhang separately.

My choice would be 12" OC with the planned blocking, then size the joists and beams for stiffness rather than using their maximum allowable spans. Without the joist size and beam/post layout, neither spacing nor extra blocking can guarantee a spring-free deck.

on.p: Favor 12" OC joists over additional rows of blocking, and keep the planned blocking. For otherwise identical framing, closer joist spacing is the more dependable way to improve firmness.
They help in different ways:

on.li: Closer joist spacing reduces the decking’s span between supports and reduces the load carried by each joist under a distributed load.

Blocking keeps joists upright and can help neighboring joists share a concentrated load. Its effectiveness depends on the connections. It does not create a supported midpoint or shorten the joists’ vertical bending span. Research on timber floors describes these distinct effects on longitudinal and transverse stiffness. Timber-floor vibration study

on.p: Assuming your joists run outward from a house ledger to a beam, your layout has roughly 12 feet between supports, followed by a 2-foot cantilever. Joist depth matters greatly over that span. Deeper joists—or an additional properly supported beam that shortens the span—can deliver a larger improvement than changing spacing alone.

For perspective, a simple beam calculation gives 25% less joist deflection under the same uniformly distributed deck load when spacing changes from 16" to 12", with joist size and span unchanged. That does not mean 25% less perceived bounce under someone’s footsteps; decking, load sharing, and beam movement also affect the result.
For your goal, I would have the designer:

on.li: Compare deeper joists with the proposed joists at 12" OC.
Check beam stiffness and spacing between posts, since beam movement affects the whole deck.

Keep the midpoint blocking and detail blocking at the cantilever’s supporting beam. AWC’s DCA 6 calls for blocking there and treats the main span and cantilever as separate checks. AWC deck construction guide, Figure 6 and Table 2

on.p: 12" OC is my choice between your two options, but joist size and beam design determine whether it will feel solid. What joist size, lumber species/grade, decking material, and beam/post layout are planned?

off.p: Assuming U.S. NEC rules: your cable sounds like SER, which cannot be installed underground—even inside conduit. With suitable replacement wiring, #2 aluminum normally supports a 90-amp feeder.

off.li: Direct burial or conduit?

off.p: Check the lettering printed on the jacket. Gray jacket with three insulated conductors and one bare conductor strongly suggests Type SE, Style SER. If so, neither direct burial nor underground conduit is permitted. Southwire’s installation guidance explicitly states this restriction.

Use conductors listed for wet locations in conduit, such as XHHW-2, or a suitable four-conductor direct-burial product. If choosing USE-2, verify additional ratings permitting the portions inside buildings; USE-2 alone is insufficient for interior wiring. Southwire’s feeder selection guide explains the distinctions.

off.li: Maximum feeder breaker?

off.p: Normally a two-pole 90A breaker, provided both ends have terminals rated for aluminum and 75°C, and no installation conditions require reducing ampacity. #2 aluminum is rated 75A at 60°C, 90A at 75°C, and 100A at 90°C. The insulation’s 90°C rating does not authorize using 100A with 75°C terminals. Southwire’s ampacity table

The special dwelling-service allowance sometimes permitting #2 aluminum at 100A generally does not apply to a garage-only feeder. A subpanel rated 100A or 125A can still be supplied through a 90A breaker.

off.li: How many 15A and 20A breakers?

off.p: There is no fixed number derived from the feeder amperage. You may install the number and types permitted by the panel’s labeling, provided the calculated load fits the feeder and the house service has sufficient capacity. Adding the branch-breaker ratings is not a load calculation.
A two-pole 90A feeder supplies up to 90A on each 120V leg; distribute loads between the legs. Continuous loads generally require sizing at 125%. Schneider explains breaker ratings per pole.

If the garage is detached, also provide two hots, an insulated neutral, and an equipment ground, keep the neutral isolated from the enclosure and ground bar, and provide a garage disconnect and grounding-electrode system. Ground rods do not replace the feeder ground. St. Paul’s garage wiring guide

Before installation, have the local inspector or electrician confirm the jacket markings, burial requirements, terminal ratings, and load calculation. As described, the underground cable choice needs changing.

on.p: Assuming U.S. NEC rules: your cable sounds like SER, which cannot be installed underground—even inside conduit. With suitable underground wiring, #2 aluminum generally supports a 90-amp feeder, subject to the conditions below.

on.li: Direct burial or conduit?

on.p: Check the designation printed on the jacket. Gray 2-2-2-4 cable with three insulated conductors and a bare grounding conductor strongly suggests Type SER. NEC 338.12(A)(2) prohibits Type SE cable underground, both directly buried and in conduit. Southwire’s SER specification

For the underground portion, use either wet-location-rated conductors, such as XHHW-2, in electrical conduit, or a listed direct-burial wiring assembly. Conductors marked USE-2/RHH/RHW-2 can cover underground and indoor portions when installed appropriately; USE-only wiring has indoor-use restrictions. Typical cover requirements are 24 inches for direct burial and 18 inches for PVC conduit, with exceptions depending on the route and local code. Protect wiring where it emerges from the ground. Southwire wiring guide, St. Paul garage-wiring guide

on.li: Maximum feeder breaker?

on.p: A 90-amp, two-pole breaker is the usual maximum for #2 aluminum with 75°C-rated terminals at both ends, provided no installation conditions require reducing its ampacity. Southwire lists #2 aluminum at 90 amps in the 75°C column. A 90°C insulation marking alone does not authorize using the 100-amp column with 75°C terminals. Southwire ampacity table

The special dwelling allowance often associated with “#2 aluminum for 100 amps” generally applies to services and feeders carrying the entire dwelling load. Your garage feeder does not qualify on that basis. Your locally adopted code edition and terminal ratings must be checked before selecting the breaker. NFPA’s 310.12 text

on.li: How many 15- and 20-amp breakers?

on.p: There is no fixed count derived from the feeder amperage. The panel’s labeling limits the permitted circuits and breaker types; the calculated load determines whether the feeder can supply them. Branch-breaker ratings may total more than 90 amps.

A 90-amp 120/240-volt feeder supplies up to 90 amps on each hot leg. Distribute the 120-volt loads across both legs, and account for continuous loads at 125% in the load calculation. Schneider Electric feeder-sizing guide

For a detached garage, also provide a four-wire feeder, separate neutral and ground bars, a bonded grounding bar, a grounding electrode system, and a building disconnect. Ground rods supplement the feeder’s grounding conductor. St. Paul garage-wiring guide

Your proposed underground setup needs different wiring if the jacket says SER. Verify the full jacket markings and have the local inspector or electrician confirm the wiring method, load calculation, and service capacity before installation.

off.p: I would anchor the rail into the concrete, using a fixing arrangement designed to bridge the roughly 70 mm of plaster and insulation. I would not rely on cavity anchors in the 10 mm plaster facing without explicit approval from the lining manufacturer for loaded wall cabinets. The French specification link hasn’t come through, so I cannot check that particular board.
The important issue is the complete load path:

off.li: Cavity-anchor ratings are conditional. A “20 kg” rating applies to specified board thicknesses, installation conditions and load directions. Several anchors close together can fail by breaking out a shared section of plaster; their capacities cannot simply be added.

Ordinary long screws into concrete leave a problem at the surface. Tightening can crush the lining, and the unsupported screw length must resist bending as well as the cabinet’s downward load and outward pull.
The insulation should not serve as structural packing. The connection needs rigid support or a rated stand-off system that transfers the loads to the concrete.

off.p: Two practical approaches are:

off.li: Purpose-designed stand-off anchors. Systems such as Fischer TherMax are made for fixing through non-load-bearing insulation into the structural wall. Their published capacities depend on stand-off distance, substrate and loading. Treat this as an example of the appropriate fixing category; the manufacturer should confirm suitability for your interior lining, sustained cabinet loads and METOD rail connection. Fischer TherMax guidance

A structural backing strip or blocks attached to the concrete. Locally remove the lining behind the rail and install suitably designed backing extending to the finished wall plane. Attach the rail to that backing. This is more invasive, but provides a direct support arrangement. The detailing should also account for thermal and acoustic bridging.

off.p: Your concern about leverage is justified, but it does not automatically mean enormous screws. Proper support across the insulation thickness changes the connection substantially. The cabinet’s lower rear contact points also resist its tendency to rotate, so those points need adequate bearing support.

Ask the installer or anchor supplier to specify the anchor type, concrete embedment, spacing, stand-off support and rail-compatible heads/washers for the total loaded cabinet run. IKEA likewise requires fixings appropriate to the wall construction. METOD installation guide

For this installation, I would accept a concrete-backed fixing detail with documented capacities—not a recommendation based solely on the cavity dowels’ “20 kg” label. Before drilling, locate reinforcement and concealed services.

on.p: I recommend fixing the suspension rail into the concrete, using a fixing arrangement designed to bridge the roughly 70 mm of plasterboard and insulation. I would not use the cavity dowels you describe as the sole support for loaded kitchen cabinets.

This matches Placo’s guidance for heavy loads on glued wall linings: anchor through the lining into the masonry behind it. Your message doesn’t include the insulation datasheet link, so I can’t verify the particular 10+60 product.

The important issue is support across the insulation thickness. Tightening a long screw against the rail can compress the wool and damage the plasterboard. The screw also carries shear and bending across that gap, alongside the outward pull caused by the cabinet’s depth.
Two practical arrangements are:

on.li: A rated stand-off fixing system anchored into the concrete. These systems are designed to carry loads through insulation. Fischer’s TherMax range illustrates the principle. Have the manufacturer confirm a model suitable for your lining, sustained cabinet loads, actual stand-off distance and METOD rail connection.

Local openings with rigid blocking secured to the concrete, bringing a solid mounting surface out to the rail. The rail then attaches to that support. A competent installer can detail this, including restoring the lining and accounting for the cabinet’s lower contact points.

on.p: Compression sleeves around concrete fixings can form part of a suitable detail, but their presence alone doesn’t establish its load capacity: the anchor, sleeve and rail connection need to work together.

Your concern about adding cavity dowels is justified. A “20 kg per fixing” rating cannot simply be multiplied by the number of screws. It depends on the specified board thickness, spacing and loading direction; closely spaced fixings share the same vulnerable sheet, and the rail does not necessarily distribute the load equally.
The 70 mm gap also does not, by itself, establish that an enormous screw is needed. The required size and spacing follow from the fixing arrangement and its rated capacity.

Ask the installer or fixing manufacturer to specify the exact anchor, concrete embedment, stand-off support and fixing spacing for the full loaded cabinet run. That gives you a checkable installation detail. A recommendation to use unspecified cavity dowels is insufficient for this wall construction.

off.p: No—you can change from RMC to EMT inside either building. EMT is generally cheaper and easier to install, and it is permitted in walls and ceilings where it isn’t subject to severe physical damage. Use a listed RMC-to-EMT transition coupling that matches your threaded or unthreaded rigid conduit. Southwire’s transition fittings are an example.
Electrical PVC conduit is another indoor option where permitted, but grounding affects that choice:

off.li: Assuming your three #6 wires are two hots and a neutral, a properly bonded, electrically continuous RMC/EMT system can serve as the equipment grounding conductor under the NEC.

If you introduce PVC, you must provide a wire equipment grounding path and bond the metal portions. For a standard 60A feeder, that is ordinarily at least #10 copper, in addition to the three feeder conductors. Grounding conductor rules, grounding conductor sizing.

off.p: For the trench, IMC is another option to price: like RMC, it generally permits six inches of cover in ordinary yard locations. PVC generally requires 18 inches. Six inches means soil above the top of the conduit, and driveway crossings have different requirements. NEC burial table.

Also, use wet-rated conductors such as THWN-2 underground. At the shed, keep neutral isolated from ground and provide the required grounding electrode system; ground rods don’t replace the feeder’s equipment grounding path. Underground wiring rules, separate-building grounding rules.
These are NEC-based rules; confirm your locally adopted requirements before buying materials.

on.p: You can transition to a cheaper wiring method indoors. Assuming U.S. NEC rules, RMC is not required all the way to both panels.

on.li: EMT (“thin-wall” metal conduit) is a practical indoor option, including concealed runs in walls and ceilings. Join it to RMC with a listed transition fitting or through a suitable box. You can keep the same conductors throughout. EMT rules, transition fittings.

Electrical PVC conduit is also generally permitted inside walls and ceilings, subject to physical-damage protection and local amendments. Switching to PVC affects your grounding arrangement. NEC Article 352 text in NFPA’s development record.

on.p: Your three-wire plan makes grounding particularly important. For a typical 120/240-volt shed feeder, you need two hots, a neutral, and an equipment-grounding path. Properly connected and bonded RMC and EMT can supply that grounding path, allowing three insulated wires. PVC cannot: if you introduce PVC, provide a grounding conductor and bond the metal portions. A continuous grounding wire alongside the feeder conductors is a straightforward choice. Steel Tube Institute grounding guidance.

For the trench, IMC is another option to price: it generally qualifies for the same six-inch cover as RMC. Ordinary buried PVC generally requires 18 inches. Six inches of *cover* means soil above the conduit’s top, so the trench must be deeper than six inches. Special locations can require greater cover; confirm your route with the inspector before buying materials. Minnesota’s NEC inspection checklist.

Use wet-location-rated conductors underground, such as THWN-2. At the shed, keep neutral isolated from the enclosure and grounding bar, and provide the required grounding electrode system; ground rods do not replace the feeder’s equipment-grounding path. Southwire wire specifications, detached-building grounding guidance.
